resources.why: Almost every job, friendship and exam interview runs on communication. Learners who can look at a listener, organise three points and speak audibly — and who listen without interrupting — are immediately distinguishable in interviews and in class.
steps: Listening first (10 min): The listening rules — eyes on speaker, mouth closed, thinking about the words, wait then ask. Demonstrate a bad listener (comic), then a good one.
Telephone game (10 min): Message relay round the class — shows how meaning corrupts without care; discuss why repetition and clarity matter.
Structure recipe (10 min): My name and topic — 3 points (First…, Second…, Finally…) — my conclusion. Learners draft a 1-minute talk on 'My best day in school' using the frame.
Speaking circles (15 min): Groups of 4 — each speaks 1 minute while 3 listeners score eye-contact, voice and structure; rotate twice.
Class showcase (5 min): 2 volunteers present to the whole class.
resources.assessment: Learner delivers a 1-minute talk using the 3-part frame while listeners report active listening.
resources.notes: Shy learners start with 30 seconds and a seated position — growth, not perfection, is the goal.

reallife.situation: A pupil mumbles an answer with eyes down and the class misses a good idea entirely.
reallife.way: Speak up, look up, say it clear - good ideas deserve clear voices. Practice makes the brave voice normal.

reallife.situation: Two friends talk over each other until both forget the point.
reallife.way: Listening is half of speaking: let the other finish, look at the speaker, then answer the point - not the volume.

activities: Clear-voice relay: deliver one idea standing tall
Listen-and-repeat pairs: summarise what you heard
Eye-contact and tone practice circuit
home: Tell your family one clear story this week - eyes up, words in order
Practise listening fully before replying, at home and in class
Report one conversation where listening won
discussion: What does a clear speaker look like and sound like?
Why is listening half the skill?
How do you disagree without shouting?
resources.encouragement: Clear voices and patient ears - the marks of future leaders! Speak so the room hears you; listen so the room trusts you. Practise both until they are yours. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Teamwork: Working Together in Groups
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner states 3 rules of good teamwork.
Learner completes a group task where every member contributes.
resources.why: From farming to football to offices, Ghanaians achieve in groups. Children who learn early to share tasks, wait their turn, include the quiet one and finish the job together carry the skill every employer and community depends on.
steps: Tower challenge (15 min): Groups build the tallest paper tower — observe and afterwards ask: who shared materials? who listened to whose idea? did anyone get left out?
The 3 rules (10 min): 1) Everyone's idea is heard. 2) Tasks are shared — everyone has a job. 3) We finish together and help anyone who is stuck.
Roles (10 min): Introduce roles — leader, materials keeper, timekeeper, presenter — and re-run a mini task with roles assigned.
Reflection (5 min): What made the best team the best?
materials: Paper, bottle tops or blocks for towers
resources.assessment: Learner states the 3 rules and their group role; every member contributes visibly.
resources.notes: Rotate roles every group task so the quiet learners get leadership turns.

reallife.situation: A group assignment collapses: everyone talks, nobody divides work, the deadline dies.
reallife.way: The team that names tasks, owners and a finisher wins. One goal written down, tasks shared by name, a check-in before the deadline.

reallife.situation: Two members quarrel over methods while the work freezes.
reallife.way: Attack the idea, never the person; then merge the best of both. The quarrel ends when the goal is read aloud again.

activities: Timed team task with division-of-roles practice
Merged-idea exercise: two plans into one
Team roles rotation drill
home: Organise one family task this week with named roles
Report how the division of work went
Practise the kind disagreement phrase at home
discussion: What makes a team actually work?
How do you disagree without wounding?
What does the quiet member of a team deserve?
resources.encouragement: Team builders, well done! The goal shared, the tasks named, the quiet one lifted - that is how houses and nations are built. Practise until teamwork is your habit. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Solving Disagreements Without Fighting
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner uses the 4-step peaceful problem-solving sequence.
Learner identifies anger warning signs and one calm-down strategy.
resources.why: Fights destroy friendships, cause suspensions and escalate into injuries — yet almost every school fight starts as a small disagreement handled badly. Learners who own a peaceful sequence (and know how to cool anger first) become peacemakers instead of combatants.
steps: Anatomy of a fight (10 min): Replay a familiar small conflict — what escalated it? (insults, audiences, pride, refusing to listen).

Calm down first (5 min): Anger signs (hot face, tight fists, loud voice) and calm-down tools — breathe slowly 5 times, walk away, count to 20, splash water. 'Never solve anything while your body is boiling.'

The 4 steps (10 min): 1) Each side states what happened WITHOUT insults (I-statements: 'I feel angry when…'). 2) Each listens and repeats the other's view. 3) Both suggest fair solutions. 4) Agree on one and shake.
Role-plays (15 min): Scenario pairs (football foul, borrowed book damaged, seat disputes) run the 4 steps; class watches for insults and fair solutions.
Peace pact (5 min): Class code — insults stop disagreements; fists end friendships.
resources.assessment: Learner runs the 4 steps in a role-play without insults and agrees a fair solution.
resources.notes: Teach bystanders too: the audience decides whether a fight happens. Laughing fuels it; 'cool it' starves it.

reallife.situation: Two pupils shove over a borrowed ruler; one is hurt and both are punished.
reallife.way: The talk-first path: state the problem, listen to the other side, agree the fix. Fists settle nothing that words cannot settle better.

reallife.situation: A disagreement over a game rule ends a friendship for a term.
reallife.way: Check the rule together, or agree to disagree and play again tomorrow. The friendship outlasts every rule dispute when pride steps aside.

activities: Talk-it-out role plays with the peace steps
Win-win solution hunt for sample conflicts
Mediation practice: a third pupil guides the talk
home: Use the peace steps in one home disagreement this week
Teach the steps to a sibling
Report one conflict words solved
discussion: Recite the peace steps in order.
Why does shoving always make things worse?
What does a good mediator listen for?
resources.encouragement: Peacemakers, stand honoured! The tongue that talks through trouble builds what fists destroy. Take the peace steps everywhere you go. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Managing My Time
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains the difference between urgent and important tasks.
Learner builds a personal after-school timetable.
resources.why: Learners who reach JHS without time habits drown in homework, chores and football. A child who plans the evening — homework first, chores, play, sleep at a set hour — walks into JHS with an advantage that lasts through BECE year.
steps: Time audit (10 min): Learners estimate yesterday's hours — school, chores, homework, play, screens, sleep. Where did it go?

Urgent vs important (10 min): Sort task cards — urgent AND important (homework due tomorrow) vs urgent only (TV now) vs important not urgent (reading daily). Homework and revision live in the important zone.
Building the timetable (15 min): Fixed items first (school, chores, dinner), then homework block, then play — each learner drafts a realistic personal evening timetable with times.
Reality check (5 min): Swap timetables with a friend — is anything impossible? Fix it.
Trial week (5 min): Run it for one week and mark each day kept/missed.
resources.assessment: Learner's timetable places homework before play, with realistic times, and the learner explains the urgent/important difference.
resources.notes: Chores are real in Ghanaian homes — plan WITH them, not against them, or the timetable dies in week one.

reallife.situation: A pupil 'planned to study' every evening and somehow never began - the phone and the yard swallowed the hours.
reallife.way: Time needs appointments, not wishes. Put study in the timetable at your golden hour, guard the block like money, and let play have its own honoured slot.

reallife.situation: A student juggles chores, homework and play until everything suffers.
reallife.way: Sequence and balance: fixed duties first, study in its protected block, play and rest honestly scheduled. A day with a shape beats a day with a struggle.

activities: Personal weekly timetable design workshop
Golden-hour identification exercise
One-week timetable run with Friday review
home: Build your weekly timetable with a parent's blessing
Protect the study block daily; tick it honestly
Review the ticks every Friday and adjust
discussion: What is your golden hour for study?
Why must play be scheduled, not stolen?
What do you do when a timetable block keeps failing?
resources.encouragement: Masters of your hours, march on! Time is the one wealth every child receives equally - and you have learned to spend it like a king. Keep the appointments; the results will follow. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Setting Goals and Building a Study Plan
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner writes a SMART goal.
Learner converts a goal into a weekly study plan with specific subjects and times.
resources.why: JHS learners carry the BECE dream — but dreams without plans stay dreams. A learner who writes 'I want aggregate 6' and then books Mathematics for Monday evenings and English for Wednesday evenings has converted hope into a schedule, which is the only thing that actually produces results.
steps: Dream to goal (10 min): Each learner names their dream (school, trade, profession) and the grades it needs. Then sharpen it SMART — Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Example: 'Score at least 70% in Mathematics by end of Term 1'.
Gap analysis (10 min): Where am I now in each subject? What is the gap? Which subjects need the most hours? (Honesty required — the plan is for them, not the teacher.)

The weekly plan (20 min): Fixed anchors first (school, chores, church/mosque), then subject blocks — weakest subject gets the best hours; every evening has ONE named subject; short breaks every 30-40 minutes; weekends for revision + rest.
Commitment (5 min): Sign the plan; choose an accountability partner who checks it weekly.
Review loop (5 min): Every Sunday — what worked, what did not, adjust next week.
resources.assessment: Learner's plan names subjects and times for the week and contains a correctly written SMART goal.
resources.notes: Print the plan and give it to the parent/guardian — home support doubles follow-through.

reallife.situation: A JHS student 'wants to pass BECE' with no plan, and panic arrives in the final term.
reallife.way: Goals need numbers and dates: 'three maths topics mastered by Friday', written where the books are. Weekly targets make the mountain a staircase.

reallife.situation: A pupil's study plan lasts four days, then vanishes.
reallife.way: Plans die when they are too grand. Three honest subjects, small blocks, ticked nightly - and the plan survives its first month, which is where most plans are buried.

activities: Goal-setting worksheet: one goal with number and date
Weekly study plan build with named topics
Progress tracking setup with self-test schedule
home: Write one study goal with a number and a date this week
Tick your study blocks nightly; review Sunday
Show the plan to a parent and ask for their blessing
discussion: Why must a goal carry a number and a date?
What makes a study plan survive past week one?
How do weekly self-tests change preparation?
resources.encouragement: Goal-setters, march on! The mountain is climbed by named steps, not by staring at the top. Write it, block it, tick it - and let every small victory recruit the next. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Exam Preparation and Calm Under Pressure
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner builds an exam-preparation countdown plan.
Learner uses 2 in-exam strategies: time budgeting and question triage.
resources.why: BECE decides school placements, and panic wastes marks as reliably as ignorance does. Learners who rehearse the exam-day routine — sleep, time-per-question, easy questions first, never leaving blanks — convert their real knowledge into real marks.
steps: Countdown plan (15 min): Working backwards from exam day — last month (cover weak topics), last week (revise notes and past questions, no new topics), last 3 days (light review, early sleep), exam eve (pack pens/pencils/rules, sleep early).

The exam-hall routine (15 min): Read instructions twice; budget minutes per question from total marks; answer EASY questions first to bank marks; mark hard ones and return; NEVER leave a blank — an attempted answer can score; keep 10 minutes to check.
Calm body (10 min): The physical tools — breathe in 4, hold 4, out 4 twice; feet flat, shoulders down; skip nothing from breakfast; no all-night cramming (sleep converts practice into recall).
Mock mini-exam (5 min): 5 questions in 4 minutes using the routine — feel the difference the strategy makes.
Debrief (5 min): What will you change about your last exam approach?
resources.assessment: Learner completes the mock mini-exam using time budgeting and scores a stated personal improvement target.
resources.notes: Normalize nerves: a racing heart means the body is ready — the routine channels it.

reallife.situation: A candidate trembles through the exam, misreads instructions and leaves easy questions untouched.
reallife.way: Calm is a skill: deep breath at the desk, instructions read twice, easiest questions banked first, hard ones flagged for later. The prepared routine outshouts the panic.

reallife.situation: A student crams past midnight and faces the paper empty.
reallife.way: The brain files knowledge in sleep; the all-nighter sells tomorrow to buy tonight. Light review, real sleep, good breakfast - the candidate arrives to collect, not to search.

activities: Timed mock paper with full exam strategy
Instruction-trap hunt on specimen papers
Reset-routine drill: pen down, breathe, restart
home: Run one timed past paper at home this week
Fix your exam-morning routine: sleep, breakfast, kit
Rehearse the reset routine twice
discussion: Why do the easiest questions come first?
What does the reset routine break?
Why is the all-night cram a bad bargain?
resources.encouragement: Calm candidates, walk in tall! You have practised the hall the way athletes practise the track - arrive with your plan, breathe through the hard, collect every easy mark. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Building Confidence and Self-Esteem
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner identifies 2 personal strengths with evidence.
Learner replaces one negative self-statement with a growth statement.
resources.why: At JHS age, self-talk becomes destiny — the learner who says 'I am just not a Maths person' stops trying, and the belief itself causes the failure. Learners who can name their strengths and re-frame weakness as 'not yet' attempt more, persist longer, and stand taller.
steps: Quiet poll (5 min): Anonymous cards — 'Write one thing you wish you were better at.' Read a few aloud; the room realises everyone carries doubts.
Strengths hunt (10 min): Each learner lists 3 strengths WITH evidence ('I am patient — I taught my younger brother to ride a bike'). Friends add one strength they see in each other.
The 'yet' skill (10 min): Reframe drill — 'I cannot do fractions' → 'I cannot do fractions YET — I will practise 15 minutes daily.' Contrast fixed vs growth statements on the board.
Confident body (10 min): Stand tall, chin up, speak at the back of the room — practise introducing yourself with the strong posture; note how it changes the feeling.
Affirmation chain (10 min): Each learner receives 2 one-line strengths from classmates to keep in their notebook.
resources.assessment: Learner states 2 strengths with real evidence and one 'yet' reframe.
resources.notes: Protect the vulnerable during the strengths exchange — model one round yourself first.

reallife.situation: A pupil answers only when certain the answer is perfect - and silence reads as weakness.
reallife.way: Confidence grows by attempted steps, not perfect ones. Raise the hand at eighty percent sure; every brave attempt compounds into the next.

reallife.situation: A student concludes 'I am just not smart' after one bad result.
reallife.way: One result is data, not identity. Skills are built by practice hours, not by birth labels - and the comeback plan turns the bad result into a map.

activities: Strengths inventory: five real abilities written and owned
Brave-attempt practice: answers at eighty percent certainty
Posture and voice practice: stand tall, speak clear
home: List three strengths with a family member this week
Practise the tall-stand and clear-voice daily
Attempt one difficult thing and report the attempt
discussion: Why is the attempted answer stronger than the silent one?
What is the difference between a result and an identity?
Name three of your real strengths aloud.
resources.encouragement: Rising stars, stand in your light! Confidence is not given - it is accumulated, attempt by honest attempt. Speak up, try again, and let practice rewrite the story. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Resisting Negative Peer Pressure
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner identifies pressure situations common at their age.
Learner demonstrates 3 refusal techniques with confident body language.
resources.why: Truancy, smoking, alcohol, gambling and early relationships rarely start with a stranger — they start with a friend saying 'just try it'. Learners who own rehearsed refusal lines and a ready exit plan keep their goals while keeping their friends where possible.
steps: Pressure map (10 min): Anonymous box — 'The hardest thing friends push you to do.' List the real pressures on the board (anonymously).
Understanding the pull (10 min): Why it is hard — fear of losing friends, wanting to belong, curiosity. Be honest: good people get pulled too.

The refusal toolkit (15 min): 1) Simple no with a reason — 'No, I have training tomorrow.' 2) Broken record — repeat your no calmly. 3) Flip the plan — 'Let's go and play football instead.' Add confident body: stand straight, eye contact, plain voice.
Pressure role-plays (10 min): Pairs act the pressure and the refusal using all 3 techniques; class scores believability.
Ally list (5 min): Each learner names 2 people they can call or sit with when pressure gets heavy.
resources.assessment: Learner demonstrates all 3 refusal techniques in role-play with confident delivery.
resources.notes: Distinguish refusing the act from rejecting the friend — 'I am not doing it' can be followed by 'but I will see you at break'.

reallife.situation: Older boys pressure a student to join an afternoon 'committee' that is really betting and smoking.
reallife.way: The plain no, the steady body, the exit: 'No - I have my plans.' Say it without essays, repeat it without anger, and leave with the friends who share your plans.

reallife.situation: Friends mock a pupil for refusing to skip prep: 'you are scared.'
reallife.way: Mockery is the pressure's second weapon; repetition is the shield. The same no, calmly, every time - and the crowd's laughter starves without new material.

activities: Refusal-scripts drill against staged pressure
The plain-no practice with settled body language
Ally planning: agree exit moves with a like-minded friend
home: Rehearse the refusal scripts aloud at home
Name the pressures you actually face to a trusted adult
Agree one ally for difficult moments
discussion: Recite the three refusal moves.
Why does the plain no beat the excuse essay?
What do you do when mockery follows refusal?
resources.encouragement: Firm-hearted ones, stand your ground! The power to refuse is the rarest power in the yard - quiet, repeatable and free. Keep your plans, keep your circle, keep your no. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Honesty, Integrity and Responsibility
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains honesty and integrity in child language.
Learner accepts responsibility for own actions in a scenario.
resources.why: Trust is the currency of every classroom, home and nation. A child who owns mistakes ('I forgot it — it was me') instead of blaming others grows into the adult who keeps promises, handles money honestly and is trusted with responsibility.
steps: Story (10 min): The child who returned the lost money — what did people say about that child afterwards?
Concepts in child words (10 min): Honest = you tell the truth even when it is hard. Responsible = you own what you did and fix what you broke.
Puppet scenarios (15 min): Puppets face choices — broke a plate, forgot homework, found a pencil — class advises each puppet and praises the responsible choice.
Class responsibility jobs (5 min): Every learner gets a small classroom duty (water keeper, chalk monitor, board cleaner) — responsibility is practised, not preached.
resources.assessment: Learner responds honestly in a puppet scenario and performs their class duty for one week.
resources.notes: When a child confesses honestly, thank the courage BEFORE addressing the fault — it keeps truth-telling alive.

reallife.situation: A boy finds money in the corridor and pockets it while the monitor's back is turned.
reallife.way: The unwatched moment is the true test. Hand it to the teacher - the owner may be crying somewhere - and let your name carry honour into every future room.

reallife.situation: A pupil breaks a window playing and lets the blame drift to the wind.
reallife.way: Own it early: what I did, why it was wrong, how I will fix it. Honest feet walk lighter than hidden ones - and repair builds more trust than innocence faked.

activities: Integrity scenarios circuit: decide before the crowd
Found-item protocol role play
Responsibility chart: my duties at home and class
home: Perform one unwatched right action this week
Own and fix one small wrong honestly
Keep one small promise exactly as made
discussion: What do you do with found money and why?
What are the four parts of owning a wrong?
Why do unwatched actions decide character?
resources.encouragement: True ones, walk tall! Character is what remains when nobody watches - and you are building a name that witnesses will confirm. Keep your hands clean and your word firm. Ayekoo!

resources.title: My Rights and Responsibilities as a Child
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner lists 4 rights of the child (Ghana's Children's Act 1992, Act 560).
Learner matches each right to a matching responsibility.
resources.why: Ghana's Children's Act (1992, Act 560) protects every child's right to life, education, health, shelter and protection from harm — but rights land best when learners see the mirror: my right to education carries my responsibility to attend and learn. Knowing both protects children from abuse AND from entitlement.
steps: Starter (10 min): 'Do children have rights? Who decides?' Introduce the Children's Act 1992 (Act 560) and the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (Ghana has ratified).

Rights gallery (15 min): Posters around the room — right to education, health care, shelter, protection from harm and forced labour, play/rest, name and nationality. Groups visit each and note examples.

The mirror (10 min): Every right has a partner responsibility — right to education ↔ go to school and learn; right to food/shelter ↔ respect and help at home; right to protection ↔ obey safety rules and report harm.
Real-life check (10 min): Scenarios — a child kept out of school to trade all day; a child beaten brutally — which rights? What should happen? (Report: teacher, Social Welfare, police).
Charter (5 min): Class rights-and-responsibilities charter signed by all.
resources.assessment: Learner lists 4 rights and pairs each with its matching responsibility.
resources.notes: Report harm through teachers or the Department of Social Welfare — give learners the real channel, not vague advice.

reallife.situation: A child is kept from school to sell on the streets daily.
reallife.way: Education is a right - and adults in the community can be reached: teachers, social welfare, trusted elders. The trained child who reports with respect opens doors for many children.

reallife.situation: A pupil demands rights but refuses every duty at home and school.
reallife.way: Rights and duties walk together: the right to learn carries the duty to try; the right to care carries the duty to respect. Balanced children are trusted children.

activities: Rights-and-duties matching table build
Community helpers identification walk
Role-play: respectfully raising a real concern
home: Name three of your rights and their partner duties
Discuss one community helper your family knows
Fulfil one duty this week without being chased
discussion: Name three child rights and their partner duties.
Whom can a child approach when a right is denied?
Why do duties make rights credible?
resources.encouragement: Young citizens, stand informed! Know your rights, wear your duties, and use your voice with respect - the balanced child becomes the community's trusted adult. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Community Service: Lending a Hand
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains what community service is and why it matters.
The class plans and completes one small community service project.
resources.why: Citizenship is a muscle — it grows only by use. A class that sweeps the clinic waiting area, reads to the KG class, or clears a choked gutter learns that 'community' is not a social studies word but a place they can change with their own hands.
steps: What and why (10 min): Community service = giving time/skill without payment. Examples: hospital/clinic help, cleaning markets and gutters, helping the aged, tree planting, neighbourhood watch support.
Needs hunt (10 min): 'What problem near our school could we fix in 2 hours with no money?' List ideas and vote.
Planning (15 min): Choose one — assign jobs, materials, date, safety rules, and what permission/adult supervision is needed.
Do it (next week — 90-120 min): Execute the project with photos for the class report.
Reflect (10 min): What changed? What did WE learn? Who noticed? (This builds the service habit, not a one-off event.)
materials: Depends on project — brooms, gloves, rubbish bags, watering cans
resources.assessment: Class completes the project and each learner states one way the community benefited.
resources.notes: Keep projects small, safe and repeatable. Invite the assembly member/chief to see the work — community recognition compounds.

reallife.situation: An aged neighbour's compound is flooded and nobody moves - the children 'have their own work'.
reallife.way: The trained class moves first: a visit, an hour, the drain cleared. Communities remember free hands - and the rememberers become the recommenders.

reallife.situation: A pupil helps only when visitors or cameras appear.
reallife.way: Service performed for the stage is theatre. The unwatched hour is the valuable one - that is where real names are minted.

activities: Community-needs map around the school
Service diary setup with reflection lines
One executed service act with written reflection
home: Perform one service act this week - unwatched
Record it and reflect: what did I learn, whom did I meet?
Plan next month's service
discussion: What does service build in the server?
Why is the unwatched act the true one?
Map three service opportunities near you.
resources.encouragement: Lenders of free hands, well done! Service is wealth deposited where interest is paid in trust and names. Serve sincerely, record honestly. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Keeping My Community Clean: Waste Management
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains how poor waste disposal causes disease and flooding.
Learner practices the waste hierarchy: reduce, reuse, recycle, proper disposal.
resources.why: Choked gutters flood Accra every rainy season and mosquitoes breed in every discarded sachet. Learners who sort waste, refuse single-use where possible, and keep their compound clean are acting on the environmental lesson Ghana most needs.
steps: The chain (10 min): Trace it — thrown sachet → choked gutter → flood → malaria/cholera → missed school. Learners draw the chain.

Sort it (15 min): Waste sorting game — organic (food peels → compost pit), plastics (reuse/recycle), papers (burn ONLY where approved — prefer reuse), hazardous (batteries, broken glass — special handling).
The hierarchy (10 min): Reduce (use less packaging), Reuse (bottles as pen holders, sachets as seedling bags), Recycle (where collection exists), Dispose properly (covered bins, not gutters/bushes).
School audit (5 min): Walk the compound — where does our waste actually go? One fix we propose this week.
Action (5 min): Class adopts the compound cleaning rota.
resources.assessment: Learner sorts 8 of 10 waste items correctly and states 2 diseases poor waste causes.
resources.notes: Composting peels into the school garden turns this lesson into free fertiliser — circular, visible, memorable.

reallife.situation: A pupil drops a sachet 'where others have dropped' and the drain beside the school slowly chokes.
reallife.way: Every drop of litter is a vote for the next flood. Bin it, bag it, or better - refuse the extra plastic at the start.

reallife.situation: The class burns refuse with plastics mixed in; smoke drifts into the classrooms.
reallife.way: Plastics never burn - they poison. Separate the waste: burnables alone, plastics bagged and binned, organics buried where approved.

activities: Waste-sorting relay: burn, bury, bin, reuse
School litter audit with a zone map
Reuse workshop: sachets into planters
home: Audit your home's waste for one week
Separate plastics from burnables every day
Run one home or street clean-up
discussion: Trace the sachet from your hand to the flood.
Recite the waste hierarchy with examples.
Why must plastics never burn?
resources.encouragement: Street keepers, stand proud! Clean compounds are the sum of ten thousand private refusals - and you have joined the refusers. Lead your homes; teach your streets. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Tolerance: Respecting Our Differences
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains tolerance and its limits (respect does not require agreement).
Learner demonstrates respectful disagreement on a real difference.
resources.why: Ghana's classrooms mix tribes, faiths, languages and abilities — and insults about tribe, religion or disability are often a learner's first experience of exclusion. Learners who can disagree without dehumanising keep the peace at home and defend it as adults.
steps: Our mix (10 min): Anonymous mapping — languages spoken at home, faiths, home regions. The class IS the diversity lesson.
Respect vs agreement (10 min): Tolerance means living respectfully WITH difference, not pretending it does not exist. Name the boundary: beliefs may differ; mocking does neither side honour.
Tribal/religious jokes audit (10 min): Learners recall common jokes/stereotypes and examine the harm — 'funny to some, degrading to the target, dangerous in a crowd'.

Practice dialogue (10 min): Pairs with different views on a mild topic (best football team, best food) must state their view AND summarise the other's fairly — the discipline of disagreement without insult.
Class covenant (5 min): One line everyone signs: 'Here, no tribe, faith or language is a joke.'
resources.assessment: Learner participates in a respectful disagreement and states the class covenant's purpose.
resources.notes: Teacher sets the tone: correct bias instantly, quietly and consistently — tolerance is caught from adults first.

reallife.situation: A new pupil speaks a different home language and the class edges her out.
reallife.way: Ghana speaks many tongues and sits at one table. Include her in games that need no long words; patience with another's difference is the mark of a trained heart.

reallife.situation: Children from two communities trade insults about food and dress.
reallife.way: Mocking another's culture mocks the whole country's wealth. The wise child answers differences with curiosity - 'show me how it is done' - and gains a friend.

activities: Tolerance scenarios sorting and discussion
Culture-sharing circle: one custom per pupil, honoured
Kindness-to-differences charter signing
home: Learn one greeting from a neighbour's language
Share one meal or custom with another community's friend
Report one moment you chose curiosity over mockery
discussion: Why does Ghana's diversity make it stronger?
What does curiosity do that mockery cannot?
How do you welcome a pupil who is different?
resources.encouragement: Children of many tongues, one family - walk in peace! Respect for difference is the flag's deepest lesson, and you wear it well. Curiosity over mockery, always. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Filling Forms and Writing a Simple Letter
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner fills a simple form completely and correctly.
Learner writes a short personal note/letter with the essential parts.
resources.why: Adult life is paperwork — school admission forms, MoMo registration, clinic cards, job applications. A learner who can read instructions, fill every field neatly and write a clear note will never need someone else to manage their own basic documents.
steps: Form anatomy (10 min): A real form projected/drawn — label fields (name, date of birth, address, signature), spot instructions ('Use BLOCK LETTERS', 'Tick one'), and the traps (empty fields, wrong date format).
Guided fill (10 min): Class fills a mock school club form together, field by field, checking each against instructions.
Neatness discipline (5 min): Write withIN lines, no crossings-out, ask before guessing, always sign where signed-off is required.
Simple letter (10 min): The 5 essential parts — date, greeting, body (why I am writing), closing, name. Write a note requesting permission for a school trip.
Check swap (10 min): Partners audit each other's form and letter against the checklist.
resources.assessment: Learner's form has zero empty required fields and the letter contains all 5 parts.
resources.notes: Bring REAL forms where possible (a blank clinic card) — authenticity makes the skill obvious.

reallife.situation: A pupil fills a form at the clinic in a hurry and the wrong entry costs the family a return trip.
reallife.way: Forms are read twice and filled slowly: capital letters where asked, one box per answer, no blanks where a dash belongs. Careful hands are trusted hands.

reallife.situation: A letter to the headmaster is written like a text message to a friend.
reallife.way: The letter has its uniform: your address, the date, the greeting, the body, the close, the signature. Dress the letter properly and doors open faster.

activities: Form-filling practice with a real-style form
Formal letter assembly drill with the full uniform
Peer checking swap with a checklist
home: Fill one real form with an adult this week
Draft one formal letter and have it checked
Practise your address and a parent's details in writing
discussion: What are the parts of a formal letter in order?
Why are forms filled slowly and checked twice?
What belongs in the closing of a letter?
resources.encouragement: Careful writers, stand skilled! The form well filled and the letter well dressed are passports that open offices quietly. Practise until precision is your habit. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Basic Cooking and Kitchen Safety
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner follows a recipe with correct sequencing.
Learner applies 5 kitchen safety rules.
resources.why: Feeding yourself safely is independence. Learners who can prepare a simple, balanced dish — and know to turn pot handles inward, cut away from fingers, and never pour water onto hot oil — protect themselves daily and impress their households within a week.
steps: Menu and maths (10 min): Choose one simple dish (e.g., plain rice and stew or groundnut soup starter) — read the recipe, list ingredients and cost them from a mock market list.
Mise en place (10 min): Wash hands, tie hair, clean the station, gather and wash all ingredients and utensils BEFORE any heat — professional habit from day one.
Safety briefing (5 min): Pot handles turned inward, knife cuts away from fingers, dry hands for electricity, fire discipline, never leave cooking unattended.
Cook (25 min): Execute step by step with roles (washing, cutting under supervision, stirring, timing).
Taste, review, wash up (10 min): Eat together, then clean the kitchen completely — cooking is not finished until the kitchen is clean.
resources.assessment: The dish is completed per recipe sequence and learners state all 5 safety rules.
resources.notes: Allergy and religion check BEFORE choosing the dish. Mix cooking with nutrition talk — protein, vegetables, less oil.

reallife.situation: A student fries alone, the oil spits, and an arm pays the price for skipped safety rules.
reallife.way: Hot oil is an angry animal: sleeves up, dry hands, no water near the pan, children supervised always. One second of obedience saves a lifetime of scar.

reallife.situation: A pupil chops without the claw grip and the knife slips.
reallife.way: The claw grip, the stable board, the sharp blade handled slowly - or the adult's hands on the task. The kitchen is a workshop: train, then work.

activities: Kitchen-safety rules drill with the five gates
Safe knife-grip demonstration on soft foods
Clean-as-you-go station practice
home: Cook one simple dish with adult supervision
Apply all five safety gates every time
Wash and store tools properly after use
discussion: Name the five kitchen safety gates.
What is the claw grip and when is it used?
Why does water never enter hot oil?
resources.encouragement: Kitchen apprentices, stand proud! Cooking well and safely is love served hot - practise the gates until they guard you automatically. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Simple Repairs: Sewing a Button and Mending a Tear
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner sews a button securely.
Learner makes a simple straight mend on a small tear.
resources.why: A torn uniform or lost button sends children to the tailor for money many families do not have — or to school looking unkempt. A learner with a needle, thread and 10 minutes of skill fixes both, and the confidence of mending one's own things lasts forever.
steps: Tools and threading (10 min): Needle, thread, scissors — thread the needle (double for strength), knot the end. Patience drill — everyone threads successfully before moving on.
Button sewing (15 min): Position, anchor stitch, pass through the button holes 4-6 times, anchor underneath, knot and cut. Partners inspect firmness.
Simple mend (15 min): Straight tear — bring edges together, anchor, straight/ladder stitch, knot on the wrong side.
Care kit (5 min): The pocket repair kit — needle, thread, spare button — every learner should know where theirs is.
resources.assessment: Learner's button survives a firm tug and the mend holds.
resources.notes: Safety with needles is non-negotiable — count needles out and in. This is a calm, meditative lesson many learners love.

reallife.situation: A pupil's uniform tears on Monday; it waits unworn for a week because 'there is no time'.
reallife.way: Ten minutes of stitch - in and out, firm knot, tidy finish - returns the uniform to service. The mend is faster than the excuse.

reallife.situation: A button pops before an inspection and the child borrows safety pins in a panic.
reallife.way: The prepared pupil keeps a mending kit and checks buttons on Sunday night. Inspection-proofing is a Sunday habit, not a Monday emergency.

activities: Button-sewing workshop with firmness test
Running-stitch tear-closing practice
Home mending kit assembly and inventory
home: Mend one garment this week
Assemble or complete the family mending kit
Check your buttons and hems each Sunday
discussion: What are the steps for sewing a button firmly?
Why does every home need a mending kit?
When do we inspect our garments weekly?
resources.encouragement: Menders and makers, stand capable! The stitch you hold today will serve uniforms, bags and households for decades. Keep the kit ready and the fingers practised. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Planting and Caring for a School Garden
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner plants a seed correctly with right depth and spacing.
The class maintains a garden bed through germination to transplanting/harvest.
resources.why: A garden teaches patience, responsibility and where food actually comes from — and it feeds the school kitchen. Children who water a bed daily and watch week by week learn agriculture, science and discipline in one living classroom.
steps: Site and soil (10 min): Choose the spot — sun, water access, fenced from animals. Test soil feel (sand/silt/clay) and plan the beds.
Planting (15 min): Choose fast, forgiving crops — okro, pepper, garden eggs, tomato, kontomire. Correct depth (2x seed size), spacing, watering-in gently. Label each bed with crop and date.
Care rota (10 min): Assign watering days/teams, weeding duty, pest watch (check leaves weekly), and a garden diary — one learner records observations each day.
Watch and learn (10 min): Set the observation routine — measure growth weekly, count leaves, note weather. Connect to Science lessons on plants.
Harvest plan (5 min): Decide together who benefits — school kitchen, tasting day, or sale into the susu fund (life-skills loop!).
resources.assessment: Learner plants at correct depth/spacing and performs their care-duty reliably over 2 weeks.
resources.notes: Start tiny — one bed beats a failed farm. Container/sack gardens work where land is scarce.

reallife.situation: A school garden bed is watered enthusiastically on Monday and forgotten by Thursday; the seedlings surrender.
reallife.way: Plants keep a schedule: morning water, mulch on weekends, weeds evicted weekly. The garden teaches the gardener constancy before it pays in vegetables.

reallife.situation: A child plants too deep in hardened soil and nothing emerges.
reallife.way: Seeds have a depth rule - about twice their size - in loosened soil. Read the seed's demands; the soil rewards those who study it.

activities: Bed preparation and seed-depth practice
Watering and mulching rota build
Garden observation journal with weekly notes
home: Tend one plant at home this week on schedule
Record height, leaves and water in the journal
Prepare one small bed or sack for next term
discussion: How deep do seeds go and why loosen the soil?
What does mulch do for the bed?
Why does the garden reward the constant gardener?
resources.encouragement: Gardeners of green things, stand faithful! The bed that is tended daily feeds the school; the habit that is kept daily feeds the life. Water, weed, watch, wait. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Storytelling Club (Lower Primary)
resources.subject: Extracurricular
outcomes: Builds oral language, listening and confidence with zero equipment.
steps: Teacher or a learner tells a short story with actions.
Learners retell the story in pairs, adding one new detail.
Weekly rotation: 'storyteller of the week' tells a family or community story.
End of term: class story festival with simple costumes from home.
resources.assessment: Participation and retelling confidence observed over the term.
resources.notes: Zero-budget activity. Links to Ghanaian Language and English oral skills.

resources.title: Junior Debate Club (Upper Primary)
resources.subject: Extracurricular
outcomes: Builds reasoning, public speaking and teamwork.
steps: Week 1: Explain what a debate is; model a simple two-side argument on a fun topic.
Week 2-3: Practise 'for/against' speaking with easy motions (e.g., 'Homework helps us learn').
Week 4: Inter-class mini debate with 2 speakers per side.
Ongoing: Rotate motions; keep speeches to 2 minutes each.
resources.assessment: Speaker clarity and use of reasons observed with the scoring sheet.
resources.notes: Feeds directly into JHS debate and public speaking.

resources.title: Inter-Class Maths Quiz League
resources.subject: Extracurricular
outcomes: Builds speed and accuracy in number work; creates healthy class rivalry.
steps: Each class selects a 4-person team.
Weekly Friday quiz: 10 questions from that week's Maths topics.
Points table kept on a class chart; winners announced at assembly.
End of term: grand final between top two classes.
resources.assessment: Team scores tracked across the term.
resources.notes: Use the same questions learners covered in lessons that week — revision disguised as a competition.

resources.title: Reading Club: Pair Reading and Book Talk
resources.subject: Extracurricular
outcomes: Builds reading fluency and a love of books with minimal resources.
steps: Set up a reading corner with any available books, charts and big books.
Pair older/stronger readers with emerging readers for 15 minutes of pair reading.
Book talk (10 min): Favourite character, funniest part, one new word learned.
Word collectors: Learners write new words on the class word wall.
Term event: Read-aloud day — teachers, parents or community members read to the club.
resources.assessment: Fluency growth tracked through pair-reading observation; number of new words collected.
resources.notes: Book scarcity is real — rotate a small 'book box' between classes and invite donations.

resources.title: Coding and Robotics Club (JHS)
resources.subject: Extracurricular
outcomes: Introduces computational thinking and block coding without expensive kits.
steps: Start unplugged: 'robot teacher' game — learners give exact step instructions to 'walk to the door' (loops, bugs and all).
Paper programming: Design algorithms on grid paper (move/turn blocks) before any screen.
Screen time (where a device exists): Scratch or Scratch-like offline app — build an animated Ghana flag or a multiplication quiz game.
Challenges: Weekly small challenges — make the sprite dance, make a quiz ask 5 questions.
Term showcase: Demo day for the whole school; parents invited.
materials: Grid paper (unplugged phase needs nothing else)
One device with Scratch offline (if available)
resources.assessment: Learner writes a correct algorithm and completes at least 2 Scratch challenges.
resources.notes: Unplugged-first means the club runs even with zero computers — upgrade when devices arrive.

resources.title: Clean School / Clean Community Campaign
resources.subject: Extracurricular
outcomes: Instils environmental responsibility with visible results.
steps: Form the committee: class reps, sanitiser/soap monitor, rota keeper.
Weekly Friday action: sweep compound, clear gutters near school, empty and clean bins.
Monthly push: community section near school — invite parents and the assembly member.
Sanitation inspection: award the cleanest class each month at assembly.
Evidence wall: photos + before/after notes displayed.
resources.assessment: Inspection scores tracked monthly; award recorded.
resources.notes: Pairs with the waste-management life-skills module for full understanding.

resources.title: Athletics Fundamentals: Sprints, Relays and Long Jump
resources.subject: Extracurricular
outcomes: Builds fitness, technique and sportsmanship for inter-house sports.
steps: Warm-up routine: jog, dynamic stretches, drills (high knees, bum kicks) — 10 min.
Sprint technique: drive-phase start from chalk lines, arm drive, finishing through the line — timed 60m trials.
Relays: 4x50m baton (or stick) exchanges — practise the give/take zones.
Long jump basics: approach run, take-off board (chalk), landing — measure and record personal bests.
Cool down + records: Keep a class PB chart; celebrate improvements, not just winners.
resources.assessment: Personal bests tracked over the term; technique observed.
resources.notes: Feed the inter-house/inter-schools sports calendar — name the squad early.

resources.title: Spelling Bee Programme
resources.subject: Extracurricular
outcomes: Builds vocabulary, spelling and stage confidence.
steps: Build the word list: pull words from each week's English lessons (10 words/week).
Weekly mini-bee: class round — say, spell, say; 3 finalists per class advance.
Word habits: teach the techniques — syllable chunking, root words, 'write it in the air'.
Term bee: top spellers compete before the school; small prizes/certificates.
Feed the district: prepare a school team for GES/inter-school spelling events.
resources.assessment: Spelling accuracy and word-list retention tracked weekly.
resources.notes: Words from lessons = revision. Keep a pronunciation guide for tricky words.

resources.title: My School Bag: Packing and Keeping It Ready
resources.why: A child who packs a bag the night before never starts the morning in a panic. This small habit teaches planning, responsibility and working smart - the bag is ready while the child sleeps, and nothing is forgotten at home.
outcomes: Pack a school bag correctly the night before, using a written checklist.
Explain why packing at night is smarter than rushing in the morning.
Keep the bag and its contents clean, complete and in one fixed place at home.
Take responsibility for books, pencils and homework without being chased.
steps: Teacher opens a school bag in front of the class and asks: 'What must be inside a school bag every day?' Children name items; teacher lists them on the board.
Class agrees on the Master List: exercise books, textbooks for tomorrow's lessons, homework, pencil(s), sharpener, eraser, ruler, reading book, water bottle or cup, handkerchief or tissue.
Teacher holds up each item and children say aloud where it goes: 'Flat things at the back, small things in the front pocket.'
Teacher demonstrates the Night Packing Routine: 1) Check tomorrow's timetable. 2) Take out what is finished. 3) Put in what is needed. 4) Z it up. 5) Stand it by the door.
Pupils practise in pairs: one calls out the checklist, the other packs an empty bag or acts it out with pretend items, then they swap.
Class makes a personal checklist on paper, copies it, and pastes it inside the bag flap or on the wall at home.
Teacher sets the home challenge: pack tonight, and tomorrow morning show a partner without opening the bag whether you remember it is complete.
Class agrees on the golden rule: 'The bag sleeps by the door, ready before I do.'
activities: Speed-packing race in pairs using the checklist - the winner is the most complete, not the fastest only.
Draw and label a school bag showing the correct arrangement of items.
Role-play the morning panic (no checklist) versus the calm morning (checklist) and compare how each feels.

reallife.situation: Ama arrives at school and her homework book is still on the table at home. The teacher is not pleased and she feels ashamed.
reallife.way: With the night-packing habit, this never happens. If it does happen, do not blame the parent - say sorry, learn the checklist, and pack it yourself tonight. One mistake can teach a lifelong habit.

reallife.situation: Kwesi loses his sharpener every week and his mother keeps buying new ones.
reallife.way: Give every small item one home: 'The sharpener sleeps in the front pocket, always.' Check the pocket every evening. Taking care of things means money stays in the family pocket for better things.

home: Pack your bag every evening with the checklist, without being reminded.
Choose one fixed place at home where the bag always stands.
Show your checklist to a parent and ask them to tick it for one week.
discussion: Why is packing at night smarter than packing in the morning?
What items are 'flat things' and why do they go at the back?
Whose job is the school bag - yours or your parent's? Explain your answer.
How does a ready bag make tomorrow's lesson better?
materials: Sample exercise books, pencil, sharpener, eraser, ruler
resources.assessment: Pupil packs a bag from a given timetable and teacher scores against the checklist. Verbal quiz: name three things that must always be inside. After one week, pupils report on the home challenge.
resources.encouragement: Look at you, packing like a real student - organized, ready, responsible! When your bag is ready, your mind is ready. You are learning one of the biggest secrets of successful people: prepare today for tomorrow. Ayekoo - keep it up!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Sweeping and Tidying My Space
resources.why: Sweeping is the first chore almost every Ghanaian child is given, but few are taught to do it WELL. Proper sweeping, gathering dust in a dustpan without spilling, and tidying after sweeping builds neatness, patience and pride in one's surroundings.
outcomes: Sweep a floor or compound correctly, moving dirt from the corners to the centre.
Gather dirt into a dustpan without spilling and dispose of it in the rubbish place.
Tidy chairs, books and footwear after sweeping.
Show pride in a clean space and explain why a dirty environment brings sickness and shame.
steps: Teacher shows two pictures or describes: a neat compound versus a dirty one. Children describe how each place feels.
Teacher demonstrates sweeping: hold the broom comfortably, sweep FROM the corners and walls TOWARDS the centre - never chase dirt from inside out.
Demonstrate the dustpan trick: sweep the heap near the pan, tilt the pan slightly, push dirt in with short strokes, do not lift a full pan too fast.
Ask: where does the dirt go? Discuss: the proper rubbish place - never the gutter, never behind the house, never burn it near people.
Pupils take turns sweeping a marked area of the classroom for one minute each, others watch and give one kind correction.
After sweeping, class tidies: straighten chairs, stack reading books, line up slippers and bags. Teacher shows how a room looks finished.
Pupils repeat the three words: 'Sweep, gather, tidy.' Teacher praises each successful turn.
Teacher gives the home challenge: sweep a space at home and show the hands - a child who sweeps has no shame.
activities: Relay: Team A sweeps and gathers, Team B checks quality with a teacher-made score sheet.
Practise the dustpan trick with beans or sand in a tray.
Sing a sweeping rhythm while working - clean, clever children work with joy.

reallife.situation: A child sweeps dirt into the gutter and rain comes; the drain blocks and water floods the path.
reallife.way: Rubbish belongs only in the proper disposal place. Every child should ask: 'If rain comes, where will my dirt travel?' Dirt in gutters brings flood and sickness - sweeping well means thinking beyond the broom.

reallife.situation: Visitors arrive and the compound is dirty. The family feels embarrassed.
reallife.way: A clean space welcomes people and speaks well of the family. A five-minute sweep every evening keeps the home always ready for visitors. Cleanliness is honour, not punishment.

home: Sweep your space at home once a day without being told twice.
Never dump dirt in the gutter or open ground - use the proper place.
After sweeping, tidy three things: chairs, your books, your footwear.
discussion: Why do we sweep from the corners towards the centre?
Where does rubbish go, and why not in the gutter?
How does a clean classroom help us learn?
What does your sweeping say about your family and your school?
resources.assessment: Practical test: each pupil sweeps a marked square and gathers dirt; teacher scores on technique, spillage and disposal. Pupils answer the three-word rule.
resources.encouragement: What beautiful work! Look at this clean floor - you did that with your own hands! A child who keeps a clean space is preparing a clean life. Do not be shy to work hard, because clean hands carry great honour. Ayekoo, my diligent workers!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Washing Plates the Right Way
resources.why: Dishwashing is one of the most useful skills at home: it keeps the family healthy and children busy doing something that truly helps. Done wrongly it wastes water and spreads germs; done rightly it is a badge of honour.
outcomes: Wash plates, bowls and spoons following the full order: scrape, soak, soap, rinse, dry, stack.
Handle a kitchen knife-free task safely and keep water and soap from being wasted.
Explain why greasy plates and leftover food must never be left unwashed.
Take a turn at home washing dishes with pride.
steps: Teacher asks: 'Who washes plates at home?' Praise the helpers; assure everyone they will all become experts today.
Teacher demonstrates with a basin, a few plates and soap: STEP 1 scrape leftover food into the bin or a bowl (never wash food down the drain).
STEP 2 soak the worst plates briefly in a little water. STEP 3 soap and wash: start with the LEAST dirty (cups, then bowls, then oily plates) so the water stays cleaner longer.
STEP 4 rinse in clean water. STEP 5 dry on the rack or clean cloth. STEP 6 stack neatly in order. Teacher repeats the chant: 'Scrape, soak, soap, rinse, dry, stack!'
Safety talk: no playing with water, stand firmly, wash knives last and only with an adult's permission, never leave soap or water on the floor to cause slipping.
Pupils wash one plate each in groups at the water source, following the chant, while others coach.
Class compares: a well-washed plate (squeaky, no grease) versus a badly washed one (slippery). Children touch and judge.
Teacher closes with the value: 'When you wash plates well, you protect your family from sickness - that is love in action.'
activities: Station practice: groups rotate through scrape - soak - soap - rinse - dry stations.
Chant and clap the six steps; then perform them without the chant to test memory.
Sorting game: which plate is washed well? Show two sample plates and let children inspect.

reallife.situation: A family eats and leaves the plates overnight. In the morning flies have visited the food remains, and someone falls sick with stomach pains.
reallife.way: Wash dishes soon after eating - before flies and germs invite themselves. The child who washes plates promptly is protecting the whole family's health. Say it proudly: 'I wash, therefore my family is safe.'

reallife.situation: Kofi rushes and leaves grease on the plates; guests use them and it shows.
reallife.way: Do it right the first time. Feel for the squeak - a clean plate does not feel slippery. Working smart means quality work, not just fast work.

home: Wash the family dishes at least twice this week, all six steps.
Never leave leftover plates overnight without asking an adult first.
Dry and stack the dishes where they belong.
discussion: Recite the six steps in order.
Why do we start washing with the cleanest items?
Why is it dangerous to leave food scraps on plates overnight?
How does washing plates show love to your family?
materials: A few used plates, cups, spoons
resources.assessment: Practical: each pupil washes one plate; teacher checks scrape, order, rinse, dry, stack. Oral: recite the six steps and give one reason prompt washing matters.
resources.encouragement: Excellent, my little chefs' helpers! Your hands made clean plates and a safe kitchen. Remember: no work is too small when it protects the people you love. Every time you wash a plate well, you are practising to run a beautiful home of your own someday. Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Folding and Keeping My Clothes
resources.why: Neatly folded clothes last longer, are easy to find, and teach children order. Many children dress rumpled simply because no one ever taught them the fold-and-keep habit. This lesson makes every child the keeper of a tidy drawer.
outcomes: Fold a shirt, trousers and underwear neatly using the demonstrated method.
Match socks and pairs before storing.
Keep folded clothes in a fixed drawer, box or shelf.
Explain how neat storing protects clothes from dirt, wrinkles and loss.
steps: Teacher shows a rumpled uniform and a folded one. Ask: which one would you like to wear on Monday? Children answer; teacher builds the case for folding.
Demonstrate the simple fold: lay the shirt flat face-down, fold both sleeves in, fold bottom up to shoulders, then fold once more. Slowly, twice.
Demonstrate trousers: hold by the waist, match the legs, fold twice. Underwear and socks: fold small and square; socks match in pairs and tuck one into the other gently.
Set the 'one home' rule: folded clothes sleep in ONE drawer or box - shoes on the rack, never mixed in.
Pupils practise folding in pairs: one folds, one inspects with a neatness checklist (edges aligned, no big wrinkles), then swap roles.
Folding contest: the neatest three wins 'Neat Folders of the Week'. Judge by looking, not speed.
Discuss: when do we fold? (Immediately after drying and ironing - not the night before school.)
Teacher gives the home challenge: fold and keep your own clothes this week without being chased.
activities: Fold-and-pass: a shirt passes down a row, each child improves one fold.
Sock-matching speed game with a pile of mixed socks.
Draw the three fold steps as a poster for the classroom wall.

reallife.situation: It is Monday and Adjoa cannot find one matching sock, so she goes to school late and untidy.
reallife.way: Fold and pair immediately after washing day. When everything has one home, mornings are peaceful. Order in the drawer brings order in the day.

reallife.situation: Yaw stuffs clothes in a box and his uniform is wrinkled and dusty for the inspection.
reallife.way: Fold properly and store away from dust. Clothes cost money - caring for them is respecting your parents' hard work.

home: Fold all your clothes after drying, before storing.
Match every pair of socks; keep everything in one fixed place.
Keep your uniform ready and flat for the next school day.
discussion: Demonstrate the shirt fold for the class.
Why is it smart to fold clothes immediately after drying?
How does a tidy drawer help your mornings?
How does folding clothes show respect for your parents' money?
resources.assessment: Practical: fold one shirt and one pair of trousers to standard. Oral: state the one-home rule and when to fold.
resources.encouragement: Beautiful folding, champions! Look how smart your clothes look now. You are learning that great people keep great order - in their bags, their books, their clothes, and their lives. Keep every corner of your world neat, and success will find a neat place to sit beside you. Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Helping in the Kitchen Safely
resources.why: The Ghanaian kitchen is the heart of the home - and also full of fire, hot oil, steam and sharp objects. Children love to help, so they must learn exactly how to help: which tasks are theirs, which are not, and the safety rules that protect little hands.
outcomes: List the kitchen tasks suitable for a Basic 1-3 child (washing, carrying light items, peeling soft foods with care, stirring cold mixtures).
State and follow the kitchen safety rules: always ask permission, keep away from fire and hot oil, never touch knives or hot pots alone, wash hands before and after.
Help prepare one simple dish task safely under supervision.
Show respectful behaviour in the kitchen - greet, offer help, thank the cook.
steps: Teacher asks: 'Who helps mama in the kitchen?' Children share their tasks; teacher affirms each one.

Safety rules are written and recited: 1) Ask before you touch anything. 2) Fire, hot oil and steam are NOT for children's hands. 3) Knives are for adults or supervised older children. 4) Wet hands never touch electricity or hot pot handles. 5) Walk, do not run, in the kitchen.
Demonstrate a safe child task: washing tomatoes, peppers and onions in clean water; draining them gently.
Demonstrate peeling soft items (boiled eggs, cooked plantain, onion skin by hand) - while a hard knife task is shown by the adult only.
Demonstrate safe carrying: hold a bowl with two hands, walk slowly, keep it away from your face and from the fire path.
Small-group practice: each group washes vegetables and arranges them on a clean tray; the adult demonstrates stirring a cold mixture like salad or batter.
Kitchen talk: greet the cook, offer help by name ('Please may I wash the tomatoes?'), and after the meal thank the person who cooked.
Class recites: 'The kitchen is a workshop - I help, I obey, I stay safe.'
activities: Safe-or-not sorting: teacher calls tasks (carrying hot soup? washing rice? touching a knife?) and children jump 'safe' or 'not safe' side.
Vegetable washing relay with clean water and trays.
Role-play greeting and offering help to a 'cook' played by the teacher.

reallife.situation: A child tries to pour hot oil from a frying pan and the oil splashes onto an arm - a painful burn that could have scarred for life.
reallife.way: Hot oil behaves like an angry animal: it jumps. Children stay two big steps from fire and hot oil and let adults pour and fry. If a burn happens, cool water (not powder, not palm oil) and tell an adult immediately.

reallife.situation: A child wants to help but grabs a knife to cut onions and cuts a finger.
reallife.way: There are many wonderful ways to help without a knife: wash, rinse, carry, stir, arrange. Do the child tasks perfectly and the cook will teach you more as you grow.

home: Offer to help in the kitchen once this week using a safe task.
Never touch fire, hot oil, pot handles or knives without an adult.
Thank the cook after every meal this week.
discussion: Name three kitchen tasks that are safe for you and three that are not.
Why must we ask permission before touching things in the kitchen?
What should you do if food is burning or a pot is falling?
How do you greet and thank the person who cooks for your family?
resources.assessment: Oral quiz on the five safety rules. Practical: wash and drain vegetables correctly, carry a bowl safely across the room.
resources.encouragement: Well done, kitchen helpers! You washed like professionals and you kept every safety rule. A child who can help in the kitchen and stay safe is a treasure to any family. Keep learning from mama and papa - one day you will cook wonderful meals for people who will praise you. Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Caring for My Shoes and Sandals
resources.why: Clean, well-kept shoes finish a smart uniform - teachers and visitors notice shoes first. Caring for footwear is also an early lesson in maintaining what you own instead of constantly replacing it.
outcomes: Clean sandals and school shoes: knock off dirt, wash and dry leather and rubber parts properly, polish where needed.
Store footwear on a rack or in one fixed place, never scattered or left in the rain.
Explain how good shoe care saves the family money.
Present neat footwear as part of a complete smart uniform.
steps: Teacher displays three pairs: dusty, muddy, polished. Children judge: which pair is ready for school?
Demonstrate cleaning rubber sandals: knock soles together outside to remove dry mud, wash with soapy sponge, rinse, dry in shade (not direct harsh sun which cracks them).
Demonstrate leather shoes: brush off dust, wipe with damp cloth, apply polish or shea butter lightly, buff with soft cloth until it shines.
Demonstrate fabric/canvas shoes: scrub gently with soap and old toothbrush, rinse, stuff with paper to keep shape, dry in shade.
Set the storage rule: every pair has a home - rack, shelf or lined by the door; never in the rain, never under the bed where damp and mould live.
Pupils practise on their own or borrowed pairs in stations; teacher inspects shine and dryness.
Discuss: shoes are checked by teachers and visitors - what do clean shoes say about you? (I am ready. I respect myself. My home teaches me well.)
Home challenge: clean all your footwear this week and place every pair in its home.
activities: Shoe-cleaning clinic: rotate through rubber, leather and canvas stations.
Shoe parade: pupils walk and stand; class claps for the smartest-presenting feet.
Sort picture cards: rainy-day care, dusty-day care, school-morning check.

reallife.situation: Kofi leaves his sandals outside overnight; rain soaks them and by morning they smell and are mouldy.
reallife.way: Bring footwear in every evening and keep them in their home. Dry them properly after rain. Damp shoes breed smell, sickness and damage.

reallife.situation: A mother keeps buying new sandals because the old ones are thrown about and cracked from sun and misuse.
reallife.way: Clean, dry, store - and the same pair lasts years. Money saved goes to books and food. Taking care of things is a way of honouring your parents' sweat.

home: Knock dirt off and wipe your footwear every evening after school.
Wash and dry all pairs properly once a week.
Keep every pair in its fixed home - never in the rain.
discussion: Describe the cleaning steps for leather shoes.
Why do we dry shoes in the shade rather than harsh direct sun?
What do clean shoes say about a pupil?
How does shoe care save your family money?
materials: Shoe rack or marked storage area
resources.assessment: Practical: clean one pair to teacher standard. Oral: state the storage rule and one way shoe care saves money.
resources.encouragement: Shine bright, my friends! Look at those smart feet - a true student walks to school in clean, well-kept shoes. You have learned to protect the things you own, and that wisdom will protect everything you will ever own: your books, your tools, your money, your name. Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Greeting Elders the Ghanaian Way
resources.why: In Ghana, a child who greets respectfully is welcomed everywhere; a child who does not is marked as untaught. Greeting is not just words - it is the key that opens doors, gifts, help and friendship. This is one of the greatest treasures our parents pass down.
outcomes: Greet elders using respectful words and body language (good morning/afternoon, slight bow or two-handed handshake).
Explain why greeting matters: it shows respect, brings blessing, and builds relationships.
Use respectful titles instead of bare first names (aunty, uncle, sir, madam, nana).
Practise greeting in different daily situations: at home, at the shop, at church or mosque, meeting a visitor.
steps: Teacher greets the class warmly in several Ghanaian languages if possible and asks: how did that greeting make you feel?
Discuss: who has been given something, helped, or smiled at simply because they greeted first? Collect real stories.
Teach the words: Good morning / Good afternoon / Good evening, and examples in Ghanaian languages children know (teacher leads, children share theirs respectfully).
Teach the body: for elders, a small bow or a gentle two-handed handshake; stand to greet when an elder enters; do not greet while sitting glued to a game.
Teach the titles: aunty, uncle, madam, sir, nana, teacher. Rule: never call an elder just by a bare first name.

Role-play circuit: (a) entering the house in the morning - greet everyone you meet in order; (b) meeting your teacher on the road; (c) the market - greet before you buy; (d) a visitor arrives - stand, greet, offer a chair.
Discuss the special case: an elder who does not answer or looks cross. Teach: we still greet politely; sometimes people carry heavy hearts - your respect remains correct.
Close with the home challenge: greet every elder you meet this week and report the responses on Friday.
activities: Greeting circuit stations with parent-teacher volunteers or senior pupils as 'elders'.
Title matching game: pictures of people (headmistress, market woman, pastor, grandfather) matched with the right respectful title.
Class praise chain: each child greets the next properly; the chain must not break.

reallife.situation: Two children want water from the same compound; one greets the owner politely and is welcomed with a smile and a cup; the other grabs and is scolded.
reallife.way: Greeting first, always. A greeting costs nothing and pays every time. It says: 'I was trained well.' Even when you are in a hurry, respect comes first.

reallife.situation: A shy child fears greeting because of a stammer.
reallife.way: Courage grows with practice. Start with a smile and a bow, then the words. Friends and teacher can practise with you daily. A respectful heart speaks in many ways - and with practice, the voice follows.

home: Greet every elder you meet this week - at home, on the road, in the market.
Practise the two-handed handshake and the small bow with family.
Use respectful titles; no bare first names for elders.
discussion: Why does a greeting matter even before you ask for something?
Show the class the respectful way to greet an elder.
What titles do we use instead of bare first names?
What do you do if an elder does not answer your greeting?
resources.assessment: Practical role-play scored on words, body and title use. Friday: children report real greetings and the responses they received.
resources.encouragement: You greeted like true sons and daughters of Ghana! People will always remember the child who respects them. Greeting has opened palaces for the humble and hearts for the shy - and it will open good things for you all your life. Keep this treasure polished every day. Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: The Magic Words: Please, Thank You, Sorry, Excuse Me
resources.why: These small words carry great power: they turn demands into requests, accidents into peace, and strangers into friends. Children who master them early are liked by teachers, family and strangers alike - and they keep friends easily.
outcomes: Use please when asking, thank you when receiving, sorry when wronging, excuse me when passing or interrupting.
Match each magic word to its moment in daily school and home life.
Deliver a sincere apology (not a mumbled one) and a sincere thank-you.
Notice and report moments when others use magic words well.
steps: Teacher acts out two requests: 'Give me water!' versus 'Please, may I have some water?' Class says which one they would answer happily.

Introduce the four magic words on the board with the rule for each: PLEASE - before you ask. THANK YOU - after you receive, even a small thing. SORRY - when you are wrong, even by accident. EXCUSE ME - when you pass between people or need to speak.
Practise tone and face: a sorry said while looking at the ground with a frown is not an apology; the class practises looking up, saying it clearly and meaning it.
Situational drill: teacher describes a moment (borrowing a pencil, receiving food, bumping someone, needing to pass a crowded row) and the class supplies the word and the full sentence.
Role-play pairs with small props; the partner grades whether the magic word was used and whether it sounded sincere.
Teach the thank-you upgrade: name the kindness - 'Thank you for sharing your water with me.' It doubles the sweetness.
Spot-the-magic-word game for the week: pupils quietly note when a classmate or family member uses a magic word and we celebrate them on Friday.
Close with the chant: 'Please and thank you, sorry and excuse me - four small keys that open big doors!'
activities: Magic-word theatre: short scenes where a rude version is acted, then corrected with magic words.
Situational charades: children act a moment, class shouts the right word.
Magic-word wall: each real use this week earns a star with the child's name.

reallife.situation: A child snatches a sharing stick and both friends end up fighting; the class loses playtime.
reallife.way: 'Please may I use the stick first, and thank you.' The same two minutes, done with magic words, keeps the friendship and the fun. Rudeness turns small things into big fights - politeness turns big things into small ones.

reallife.situation: A child breaks a friend's pencil by accident and hides it, fearing trouble.
reallife.way: Own it quickly: 'I am sorry, I broke your pencil by accident. May I bring one to replace it?' Hiding makes it worse; honest sorry plus a plan to fix it earns double respect.

home: Use all four magic words at home this week; count your uses.
Give one full thank-you that names the kindness.
Report your best magic-word moment on Friday.
discussion: When exactly do we use each of the four magic words?
What makes an apology sound sincere?
How can a thank-you be upgraded to be even sweeter?
What happens in a family or class where nobody uses magic words?
materials: Star stickers or drawings for the wall
resources.assessment: Role-play score: correct word, correct moment, sincere tone. Weekly wall of stars records real usage.
resources.encouragement: You now carry four magic words that kings and elders love to hear! People never forget how you make them feel, and these words make others feel respected and valued. Use them at home this week and watch faces soften. Well done, my courteous champions - Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Being a Good Guest and a Good Host
resources.why: Visiting and receiving visitors are central to Ghanaian life. A child who knows how to behave as a guest - and how to welcome visitors at home - carries the family's good name wherever they go.
outcomes: Behave correctly as a guest: greet everyone, wait to be offered a seat, do not touch or eat without being offered, thank the host on leaving.
Welcome visitors at home: stand to greet, offer a seat, offer water, inform an adult.
Explain why a visitor is treated with honour in our culture.
Practise polite leaving: thank, greet, and leave at a good time.
steps: Teacher tells a short story of a child who visited a relative: list everything the child did (good and bad) from the story.

Guest rules built with the class: 1) Greet at the door. 2) Sit only where/when offered. 3) Touch nothing without asking. 4) Eat or drink only what is offered. 5) Speak politely, not loudly. 6) Thank the host when leaving. 7) Go home at a good time - do not overstay.
Host rules built: 1) Stand and greet the visitor warmly. 2) Offer a seat. 3) Offer water while waiting. 4) Call the adult. 5) When leaving, guests are escorted or told 'come again'.
Discuss: why do we honour visitors? (A visitor may have walked far; a visitor carries our name back home; kindness today brings help tomorrow.)
Role-play A: Kwame visits Aunty's house - class plays Aunty and coaches Kwame's every step.
Role-play B: a visitor arrives at Nana Ama's home while mother is in the kitchen - Nana Ama must hold the fort.
Special teach: 'No, thank you' - a guest may politely refuse what is offered; refusal must be gentle, never rude or greedy grabbing.
Home challenge: next time you visit or host, perform your role and report on Friday.
activities: Guest-and-host relay: pairs swap roles after each scene.
Draw and caption: 'My visitor checklist' and 'My guest checklist' for home display.
Story circle: children tell of a kind host or a fun visit and what made it good.

reallife.situation: A child visits a friend and starts opening cupboards and eating from the fridge uninvited; the family whispers about it for months.
