reallife.way: A guest's hands wait to be invited. Everything in another person's home is offered, not taken. One bad visit can close a door to a whole family; one respectful visit opens it forever.

reallife.situation: A visitor arrives and the child just stares at the stranger and runs away.
reallife.way: Stand, greet, offer a seat and water, then call the adult. Even small children can be graceful hosts - and elders always remember the child who welcomed them well.

home: Practise your guest checklist on your next family visit.
Welcome the next visitor to your home with greeting, seat and water.
Tell the class what happened on Friday.
discussion: Name five guest rules and three host rules.
Why are visitors treated with honour in our culture?
How do you politely refuse something you do not want?
What should you do if a visitor arrives when adults are busy?
resources.assessment: Role-play scored on greetings, seating, offers, thanking. Checklist posters assessed for accuracy.
resources.encouragement: Wonderful hosting and visiting, children! You represented your families beautifully. Remember: guests are blessings, and a warm welcome is a gift that costs nothing but means everything. Wherever you go, be the guest everyone invites back and the host everyone praises. Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Standing for the Anthem and the Flag
resources.why: The anthem and the flag are not just school routine - they honour the people who built and defended Ghana. Children who stand tall and sing with understanding learn citizenship, pride and respect for something bigger than themselves.
outcomes: Stand correctly for the anthem and flag: feet together, still, eyes forward or on the flag.
Sing the first verse of the national anthem clearly and with respect.
Explain simply what the flag's colours and star represent.
Behave respectfully during the anthem wherever it is played - not only at school.
steps: Teacher asks: why do we stop, stand and sing every morning? Open discussion; guide to the answer: we are honouring Ghana and all who served it.
Practise the standing posture: heels together, shoulders back, hands still at the sides, eyes forward. Hold for 30 seconds; anyone who giggles tries again kindly.
Teach the anthem line by line (first verse), discussing the meaning of key words simply (arise, joy, loyally). Sing together until steady.
Teach the flag colours simply: red for the blood of those who fought for us, gold for our riches, green for our land and farms, black star for African freedom and hope.
Practise the assembly flow: stand, still, sing, then the national pledge (if used), all without pushing or chatting.
Role-play: the anthem plays at a public event (sports match, ceremony) - what do you do even if others around you are talking? You stand still; your respect does not need company.
Discuss respect for the flag: never let it touch the ground, never use it as a toy or wrapper.
Close: tomorrow at assembly, the class will show Ghana how Basic 1-3 stands. Make it a point of pride.
activities: Posture drill game: longest still-and-proud stand with gentle music.
Colour and label a Ghana flag; each pupil explains one colour to a partner.
Singing circle: class sings the anthem verse as one strong voice.

reallife.situation: During a community ceremony the anthem plays; adults are talking, but one small girl stands still and sings. The master of ceremonies points her out with praise.
reallife.way: Respect is measured when others forget it. Even if nobody stands around you, you stand - because the anthem is not for the crowd, it is for your heart and your country.

reallife.situation: Some pupils wave flags as toys at a match and let them fall in the mud.
reallife.way: The flag carries the honour of our heroes. Hold it high, keep it clean, never trample it. Honouring the flag is honouring the people whose sacrifice gave us this freedom.

home: Teach a family member the first verse of the anthem.
Tell your family what the flag colours mean.
Notice the next time the anthem plays outside school - and stand.
discussion: Show the correct standing posture for the anthem.
What does each flag colour stand for?
What do you do if the anthem plays and others are not standing?
Why should the flag never touch the ground?
materials: Audio of the anthem if available
resources.assessment: Posture check at next assembly. Oral: state one colour meaning and one anthem line. Drawing assessed for correct colours and order.
resources.encouragement: You stood like true Ghanaians today - steady, proud, respectful! Our heroes and our first leaders would be glad to see you. Love for country starts in small acts like these, and you have shown you are ready. God bless our homeland Ghana - and God bless you, my young patriots. Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: How to Make a New Friend
resources.why: Many children stand alone at break simply because nobody taught them the first words of friendship. Learning to introduce yourself, ask to join and show kindness turns lonely playgrounds into happy ones - for you and for others.
outcomes: Introduce yourself to a new classmate with a smile: name, class, a friendly question.
Ask politely to join a game or share a seat.
Show the three friendship starters: smile, greeting, kind offer.
Include a child who is alone in play or conversation.
steps: Teacher asks: who remembers being the new child? How did it feel? Children share; empathy opens the lesson.
Teach Friendship Step 1: smile and say hello. 'Hello, I am Akosua. What is your name?' Practice with three different partners.
Friendship Step 2: ask a question or offer something. 'Do you like football?' 'Can I sit here?' 'May I play too?'
Friendship Step 3: share - a pencil, a story, a space on the playing field. Sharing is friendship's first food.
Discuss what pushes friends away: snatching, boasting, rude words, joining and leaving whenever convenient.
Role-play the lonely corner: one child stands alone; another must walk over and use all three steps. Rotate so everyone practises both roles.
Discuss the shy child and the child who speaks a different language at home - friendship needs patience and simple kindness, not perfect words.
Class pact: this week, nobody at break eats or plays alone unless they choose to. Friend-spotters look out for anyone standing alone.
activities: Name-and-smile chain: greet, shake, give your name and one favourite thing.
Role-play circles: lonely child, friendly child, coach who checks the three steps.
Friendship poster: 'Our class is a place where nobody is left alone.'

reallife.situation: A new pupil joins mid-term, sits alone for a week and cries quietly at break.
reallife.way: Every class member is a friend-maker. Walk over, smile, give your name, ask them to play. One child's welcome can change a whole school life.

reallife.situation: Children tease a pupil who cannot speak English well and leave her out of games.
reallife.way: Friendship is not language, it is kindness. Include her in games that need no long talk. Patience with another's weakness is the mark of a good heart - and today's patient friend may be tomorrow's helper in need.

home: Introduce yourself to one new person this week (class, church, neighbourhood).
Invite a quiet classmate to play or sit with you at break.
Tell the class one new friend's name and what you learned about them.
discussion: Say the three friendship starters in order.
How does it feel to be left alone? What can you do about it for others?
What should you do if your first hello is ignored?
Why is sharing called friendship's first food?
resources.assessment: Role-play observed on the three steps. Friday report: names of new friends made and one thing learned about each.
resources.encouragement: Look how many friends you have made in one lesson - and think how many you can make in a year! A kind word and a warm smile can turn a stranger into a brother or sister. Keep your eyes open for anyone standing alone; be their hero. Ayekoo, my friendly stars!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Sharing and Taking Turns
resources.why: Fights among young children are mostly about things: the ball, the seat, the pencil, the food. Children who learn to share and wait their turn calmly keep friends, avoid punishment, and build the patience that school and life will demand later.
outcomes: Take turns calmly in games and with shared materials, using agreed order.
Share personal items with classmates in a fair, kind way.
Use the turn-taking words: 'May I have a turn after you?' and 'It is your turn.'
Explain how sharing and turn-taking prevent fights and grow friendships.
steps: Open with a real class problem (anonymised): the ball fight at break. Ask: what started it? What could have stopped it?

Teach the Turn Rules: 1) First come, first served - but not forever. 2) Ask, do not snatch: 'May I play after you?' 3) Wait your turn without pushing. 4) Pass it on when your time ends. 5) The small sharing rule: what is mine I can offer; what is yours belongs to you until offered.
Practise the request sentence in chorus and in pairs: 'Please, may I have a turn after you?' and the kind reply: 'Yes, after me.'
Demonstrate with one ball or one marker: the class passes it in a circle using the words. Practice until calm and smiling.
Play a quick turn-based game (passing challenge or puzzle piece by piece) where the ONLY way to win is to pass correctly.
Discuss the difference between sharing (offering mine) and grabbing (taking yours). Why does grabbing cause tears? Why does sharing cause smiles?
Handle the hard case: someone never gives a turn. Teach the polite steps: ask, wait, then tell the teacher - never snatch.
Home challenge: practise one shared thing at home each day (TV remote, bathroom, serving food) using the turn words.
activities: Turn-taking ball circle with a timer - pass when the count ends.
Share-or-snatch sorting game with picture cards.
Pair practice: one child has one pencil, two need it - act it out with the magic sentence.

reallife.situation: Two boys push and shove over the only seat in the shade; one falls and cries; both miss their games.
reallife.way: Sharing the seat or taking turns by the clock keeps both happy. Snatching wins a moment and loses a friend. Ask, offer, wait - the calm child always ends up better off.

reallife.situation: A child refuses to share his crayons all term and slowly finds nobody wants to sit with him.
reallife.way: Friends are built with shared pencils, shared stories, shared jokes. A sharing heart collects friends; a gripping heart collects loneliness. Start small - share one crayon tomorrow.

home: Practise taking turns at home this week: TV, bathroom, serving food.
Share one of your things with a sibling or friend and notice the result.
Report one happy sharing moment on Friday.
discussion: Recite the five Turn Rules.
What is the difference between sharing and snatching?
What do you do if someone will not give others a turn?
How does a sharing heart make school life sweeter?
resources.assessment: Observed turn-taking in a game: correct words, no pushing, fair passing. Oral: state one turn rule and the sharing sentence.
resources.encouragement: What generous hearts you have! You passed, you asked, you waited, you shared - and look how peaceful and joyful our classroom became. Children who share are never poor in friends. Keep practising these turns at home and at play. Ayekoo, my fair and kind champions!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Kind Words Build Friends; Unkind Words Break Them
resources.why: Children discover early that words can wound deeper than sticks - and that the same tongue can heal. Teaching kind speech early stops teasing culture before it starts and builds a classroom where every child feels safe.
outcomes: Give at least five kind words or compliments naturally (well done, you can do it, sorry about that, good morning, I like your idea).
Identify unkind words (name-calling, mocking, laughing at mistakes) and their effects.
Replace an unkind word with a kind one in practice scenes.
Commit to zero name-calling in the class for one week.
steps: Teacher demonstrates with two paper hearts: kind words fold it beautifully; unkind words crease it. Unfold at the end: the creases remain - that is what harsh words do to a heart.
Collect kind words from the class onto the board: well done, sorry, you tried, come and play, well said, thank you.
Collect unkind words children hear around (without naming any pupil): stupid, useless, mocking names for body or family, laughing 'ha-ha you failed'.
Discuss the effects: unkind words make children afraid to answer, afraid to come to school, ashamed of their clothes or family. Nobody learns well with a wounded heart.
Practise the switch: teacher calls an unkind line ('You failed again, fool!') and the class transforms it into kind speech ('You will get it next time - let us practise together.').
Role-play the wounded friend: what do you do when you hear someone mocked? (Do not laugh; say a kind word to the hurt child; tell the teacher quietly.)
The Kindness Challenge board: every kind word witnessed this week is written with the speaker's name; Friday counts the score against name-calling.
Close with a class chant: 'My mouth builds, my mouth blesses - my words will not break my brothers and sisters!'
activities: Paper heart demonstration and class discussion of the creases.
Word-switch relay: teams race to convert unkind lines into kind ones.
Kindness spies: pupils catch classmates doing verbal kindness and report for the wall.

reallife.situation: A pupil wets himself in class; children laugh and give him a mocking nickname that follows him for years.
reallife.way: Laughter at a person's misfortune is a wound that never fully heals. The kind class says nothing to mock, helps quietly, and tells the teacher so the child gets help with dignity. Choose to be medicine, not mockery.

reallife.situation: A child tells another 'your family is poor' about old shoes.
reallife.way: Family wealth is never a child's fault or a child's weapon. The reply of the wise: 'My shoes will shine, and my mind will shine too.' Teachers must hear about such words the same day.

home: Say at least three kind sentences to family members each day this week.
Refuse to join any teasing or mocking; walk away and tell an adult.
Bring your kindest word of the week to class on Friday.
discussion: List five kind words and three unkind words.
What does the creased paper heart teach us?
How do you help a classmate who is being mocked?
What kind words can you say to someone who failed a test?
resources.assessment: Word-switch practice observed and scored. Weekly kindness board reviewed Friday.
resources.encouragement: You have learned the secret power of the tongue! From today your mouths are builders, not breakers. Kind words made our classroom warmer in one lesson - imagine a whole term of this! I am proud of every one of you. Speak blessing, children - Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: When Someone Upsets Me: Use Words, Not Fists
resources.why: Anger arrives fast in young children and fists follow. But fighting always makes things worse: injuries, punishments, broken friendships. Children who learn to pause, speak and report solve problems and stay out of trouble - at school and at home.
outcomes: Use the calm-down steps when angry: stop, breathe, count, walk away.
Express anger with words ('I am angry because...') instead of hitting or throwing.
Seek adult help calmly when a problem cannot be solved alone.
Explain why fighting always makes a bad situation worse.
steps: Teacher mimes getting angry (someone snatches a pencil) and the class watches the body: hot face, tight hands. Everyone learns to notice the warning signs.
Teach the four calm-down steps with actions: STOP (freeze), BREATHE (three slow breaths), COUNT (1-2-3-4-5), WALK (move away from the trouble).
Teach the words of anger: 'I feel angry because you took my pencil. Please give it back.' Practise the sentence in pairs - the voice stays firm but not screaming.
Teach the last resort: if the person will not listen, go to the teacher or a trusted adult and explain calmly. Telling is not weakness - it is wisdom.
Role-play cycle: snatching, name-calling, accident (bumped and food spilled), losing a game. Rotating pairs act the peaceful response each time.
Discuss what fighting costs: somebody bleeds or breaks, somebody cries, both are punished, friendship is damaged, and the original problem remains unsolved.
Teach the forgiveness step: after a sorry is given, we accept, shake and continue - we do not store yesterday's anger for tomorrow's fight.
Class pledge on the wall: 'In this class we use words, not fists. We stop, we breathe, we speak, we tell.'
activities: Freeze-and-breathe drill: teacher calls a provocation, children freeze, breathe and answer with the sentence.
Anger thermometer drawing: children draw their angry body and their calm body.
Peace-court role play: two 'fighters' present their case to a 'wise judge' panel of classmates.

reallife.situation: Two friends fight over a broken toy; one pushes, the other falls and is hurt. Both are punished, both cry, and the toy is still broken.
reallife.way: Stop first. Speak: 'I am angry - you broke my toy and did not say sorry.' If words fail, tell the teacher. The toy could have been mended and the friendship kept; fists make both impossible.

reallife.situation: An older pupil takes a younger one's snack daily and the younger child finally hits back with a stone.
reallife.way: Never trade a slap for a stone - reporting is stronger. The younger child should tell a teacher or parent on day one; bullies fear being seen. Adults must act; children must tell, not bleed.

home: Practise the calm-down steps at home when upset; teach them to a sibling.
Use the 'I feel angry because...' sentence at least twice this week.
Report one situation where words beat fists.
discussion: Say the four calm-down steps with actions.
Give the peace sentence for a snatched pencil.
Why is telling the teacher wisdom and not weakness?
What does fighting cost both sides?
resources.assessment: Freeze-and-breathe drill participation. Role-play scored: correct steps, correct sentence, correct help-seeking.
resources.encouragement: Powerful lesson, peacemakers! You now hold a strength stronger than any fist - self-control. Great leaders, great teachers, great parents all learned to cool the fire before it burned the house. Practise your steps until they are automatic. Ayekoo, my wise and strong children!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: My Daily Clean Routine: Bath, Brush, Wash, Wear
resources.why: Body cleanliness protects health, earns respect, and gives a child quiet confidence in class. This lesson builds one fixed daily routine - morning and evening - so cleanliness becomes automatic, not a punishment from mama.
outcomes: Follow a complete daily hygiene routine: bathe with soap, brush teeth morning and night, clean nails, wear clean clothes.
Order the routine steps correctly and explain why each one matters.
Identify the signs of good personal hygiene (clean body, breath, nails, uniform).
Own the routine personally instead of waiting to be chased.
steps: Teacher asks: how do we know a pupil is clean? Collect signs: no body smell, clean uniform, fresh breath, short nails, combed hair.

Build the Morning Routine chart: 1) Wake early. 2) Wash hands and face. 3) Bath with soap - face, underarms, private parts, feet. 4) Brush teeth (two minutes, twice a day). 5) Clean, ironed uniform and combed hair. 6) Short, clean nails. 7) Light breakfast. 8) Out early.
Build the Evening Routine: remove uniform and fold it (link to LS-LP-004), wash hands and face, brush teeth before bed, sleep in clean clothes on a clean sleeping place.
Demonstrate correct brushing: small circles, all sides, front and back teeth, tongue lightly, spit and rinse - and never share a toothbrush.
Nails and hair: trim weekly; dirty long nails carry germs straight to the mouth; lice and dirt in unkempt hair spread to friends.
Private-parts hygiene taught matter-of-factly: wash daily, dry well, tell a trusted adult about pain, rashes or anything strange. Nobody touches you there - link to LS-SAF-004.
The body-check game: partner pairs give each other the 'school ready check' - hands, nails, uniform, hair, shoes - with kind corrections.
Home challenge: follow the full routine for seven days using a chart ticked by a parent or guardian.
activities: Routine ordering cards: arrange mixed steps into morning and evening order.
Partner body-check game with the ready check sheet.
Draw the daily routine as a seven-day tick chart to take home.

reallife.situation: A pupil with unwashed uniform and strong body smell sits alone; classmates avoid him and he stops raising his hand.
reallife.way: Cleanliness restores confidence fast: bath, soap, clean cloth, and within days friends return. If washing is hard at home (no water, no soap), speak to the teacher privately - schools can help; never suffer in silence.

reallife.situation: A girl skips brushing at night 'just today' and within a week tooth pain costs her class days and a filling.
reallife.way: Two minutes twice a day beats toothache, dentist bills and missed lessons. Habits decide health - brush tonight, smile tomorrow.

home: Tick the routine chart morning and evening for seven days.
Brush twice every day; trim nails on the weekend.
Ask a trusted adult for help with anything unusual - pain, rash, smell.
discussion: Recite your morning routine in order.
Why brush twice daily and never share a toothbrush?
Why do dirty nails and hair trouble you and your friends?
Whom do you tell if something hurts or looks strange on your body?
resources.assessment: Routine chart returned after seven days. Ready-check game observed. Oral: order of steps and two reasons hygiene matters.
resources.encouragement: Fresh, clean, confident - that is you now! When you care for your body, you tell the world you respect yourself, and people always respect a child who respects themselves. Keep the routine ticking for thirty days and it becomes yours forever. Ayekoo, my sparkling students!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Do Not Take Gifts from Strangers
resources.why: Sweet words, sweets, lifts and 'your mother sent me' are among the oldest tricks used to harm children. Children must learn early: strangers offering gifts or rides are danger, no matter how kind they look or what they promise.
outcomes: State the rule firmly: never accept gifts, sweets, lifts or errands from strangers.
Recognise stranger tricks: 'I have sweets', 'Your mother sent me', 'Help me find my dog', 'Come, I will buy you something'.
Practise the safe responses: say no loudly, walk away towards known adults, scream and run if grabbed.
Identify trusted adults to run to (teacher, parent, market woman known to family, police officer).
steps: Teacher asks: who is a stranger? Guide to the truth: a stranger is anyone you and your parents do not know well - even someone who smiles and knows your name.
Present the tricks one by one (role-played by the teacher or a senior pupil): free sweets; 'your mum asked me to fetch you'; 'help me look for my puppy'; 'come, I have a surprise in my car'.
For each trick, the class answers with the Safe Response: STOP - do not take it. SAY: 'No! My mother did not send you.' MOVE: walk quickly to a known adult or back into school/home.
Teach the emergency trio: SCREAM loudly ('This is not my father!'), RUN towards people, TELL a trusted adult immediately. A child fighting silence alone is in danger; loud and fast is safe.
Teach the walk-home wisdom: move in groups, take known routes, never accept shortcuts or detours, and never keep a stranger's secret.
Trusted-adults map: each child names three safe people (parent, teacher, known neighbour, police) and where to find them.
Full role-play drill: stranger offers biscuit at the school gate - children rehearse stop, say no, move, tell.
Class pledge: 'My body, my safety, my rules: no gifts, no lifts, no secrets from strangers.'
activities: Trick-or-safe role play: adult helpers attempt the classic tricks; children rehearse refusals.
Draw the trusted-adults map for the route home.
Chant practice of the emergency trio with actions.

reallife.situation: A friendly man gives children biscuits near the school gate and later asks one girl to come to his car to see puppies.
reallife.way: Never follow. Scream 'NO!', run back to the teacher or crowd, and report every word at once. Kind faces can hide bad hearts - the rule protects you even from friendly faces.

reallife.situation: A stranger tells a boy, 'If you tell anyone, I will beat you,' after grabbing his hand.
reallife.way: That fear is a trap; secrets about strangers must burst out loud. Tell your parent or teacher immediately - adults will protect you, and children who report are heroes, not traitors.

home: Tell your family today's rule and agree your home route and trusted adults.
Walk in groups where possible; never accept lifts or gifts on the way.
Report any stranger approach to your parents the same day.
discussion: Repeat the three emergency actions: scream, run, tell.
Name three tricks strangers use.
Who are your trusted adults and where do you find them?
Why do we never keep a stranger's secret?
resources.assessment: Role-play response scored on stop - say no - move - tell. Oral recall of the three tricks and the emergency trio.
resources.encouragement: You are now safety-smart and you showed it boldly! Remember: a child who shouts and runs to a trusted adult cannot be defeated by tricks. Practise it until it is automatic, teach it to your little brothers and sisters, and stay alert every day. Ayekoo, my brave protectors of yourselves!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Fire, Stoves and Hot Things Are Not for Play
resources.why: Fire and hot liquids injure many Ghanaian children every year - from cooking fires, kettles, lanterns and candles. Children who learn the safety distance rules and what to do in a burn emergency protect themselves and their little siblings.
outcomes: Keep safe from fire, hot oil, boiling water, kettles, lanterns and matches: never touch, never play, never cook without an adult.
Know the burn first response: cool water on the burn, tell an adult immediately - no powder, no palm oil, no toothpaste.
Know what to do when fire breaks out: shout 'FIRE!', leave at once low and fast, never hide, never return for belongings.
Explain why matches, lighters and candle play are forbidden.
steps: Teacher shows pictures of a kitchen fire, a boiling pot and a lantern. Ask: which of these can hurt a child? All - and worse.

Rule set one - PREVENT: never play with matches, lighters or candles; never cook alone; keep sleeves away from flames; never run while carrying hot water; wet floors and hot oil splash - keep children away from the frying path.

Rule set two - RESPOND to burns: cool the burn under clean running or poured cool water for a long time (until help comes), remove rings/watches near it, tell an adult at once. NEVER apply powder, palm oil, toothpaste or egg - they trap heat and bring infection.

Rule set three - ESCAPE: shout 'FIRE!' loudly, crawl low under smoke (cleaner air is near the floor), leave the house quickly by the planned way out, never hide under beds or in cupboards, never go back inside for books, toys or money.
Simple home-fire plan talk: know two ways out, agree the family meeting point outside (e.g., the mango tree), fire is fought by adults and fire service - children's job is to escape and report.
Practise the escape walk: crouch low, move fast to the door, out to the agreed meeting point; repeat as a whole-class drill.
Discuss lantern and candle care at night: stand them firm away from curtains and beds; never carry a burning lantern while running or sleeping.
Pledge and poster: 'Fire is a good servant but a bad master - I watch it, I do not play it, and when it misbehaves I escape and tell.'
activities: Escape drill with the class crouch-walking to a marked meeting point.
Burn-response sorting: correct care (cool water, tell adult) versus dangerous myths (powder, oil, toothpaste).
Danger-spotting poster: pupils mark safe and unsafe spots on a picture of a kitchen.

reallife.situation: A child plays with a box of matches near the storage room and a fire starts; panic and smoke cause serious harm.
reallife.way: Fire is never a toy - one match can destroy a home in minutes. If you see smoke or flames: shout FIRE, get out low and fast, and call adults. Never touch matches anywhere, any day.

reallife.situation: Hot water spills on a younger sibling and the older child rubs powder and oil on it, making it worse.
reallife.way: The correct care is long, cool water and an adult immediately. Old remedies trap heat and cause infection. Teach this to everyone at home - it can save a baby brother or sister.

home: Learn the family escape plan: two ways out and the meeting point.
Never touch matches, lighters, kettles or pot handles; tell adults about any fire danger you see.
Teach the burn rule (cool water only, tell an adult) to someone at home.
discussion: What do you shout and where do you go when fire starts?
Why do we never hide during a fire?
What are the three wrong things people put on burns?
Why are matches and lanterns not toys?
materials: Charts for the three rule sets
resources.assessment: Escape drill performed. Sorting game scored. Oral: the escape trio and the three forbidden burn remedies.
resources.encouragement: You are now little safety officers with big knowledge! Most fire tragedies can be prevented by exactly the rules you learned today. Share them at home tonight - your words may save a family. Stay alert, stay low, stay loud in emergencies. Ayekoo, my safety heroes!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: What to Do When You Get Lost
resources.why: Markets, lorry stations and big crowds can swallow a child in seconds. A trained child who stays calm, stays put, and seeks the right help is found quickly; a wandering, crying, accepting-lifts child is in danger. Preparation turns panic into a plan.
outcomes: Memorise the Lost Plan: stop, stay, look for a safe helper, give parent's name and number.
Identify safe helpers (shopkeeper, uniformed officer, mother with children) versus risky strangers.
Never wander off searching, never accept a lift, never leave with someone claiming 'your parents sent me'.
Know personal details: parent's full name, phone number, home area.
steps: Teacher tells the story of a child lost at Kejetia or Makola market - feelings first: fear, tears, the temptation to wander.

Teach the Lost Plan in order: 1) STOP - do not run around. 2) STAY - stand at a safe open spot; people search near where you were last seen. 3) LOOK - choose a safe helper (a shopkeeper behind a counter, a police officer or soldier in uniform, a mother with children). 4) SPEAK - 'Please, I am lost. My mother's name is..., her number is...'. 5) WAIT with that helper until family comes.
Practise the data: every child recites a parent/guardian's name and phone number (if known) and their home area. Those who do not know yet get a homework mission to memorise it this week.

Who is a safe helper? Discuss and sort: uniformed officers, shop mamas, mothers with children - yes; lone strangers offering gifts or lifts - no. Anyone who says 'come with me, I will find your mother' away from the crowd - NO.
Drill the sentence until it flows: each child states their guardian's name aloud in the practice circle (privacy respected - children may whisper or write it if preferred).
Role-play stations: lost at the market, lost at the lorry station, lost at a funeral crowd - each child performs stop - stay - safe helper - speak.
Teach the special rule for shops and events: agree a meeting point with your parents BEFORE entering anywhere busy.
Class commitment: recite the plan and teach it tonight to your family.
activities: Memory drill: guardian's name and number recited in pairs until fluent.
Helper-sorting game with picture cards.
Lost-scenario role plays at three stations.

reallife.situation: A boy realises he cannot see his mother in a crowded market. He wanders street to street crying, moving farther away, and strangers keep 'helping' in confusing directions.
reallife.way: Stop and stay put. Searchers return to the last place the child was seen. Choose the market woman at her stall, state your parent's name and number, and wait there. Standing still is not giving up - it is the smartest move.

reallife.situation: A kind-looking woman tells a lost girl, 'I know your house, come with me,' away from the crowd.
reallife.way: Never leave the public place with a stranger. Ask her to come WITH you to the shop mama or police post instead. Safety loves crowds and light; danger loves quiet corners.

home: Memorise your guardian's full name and phone number this week.
Agree a family meeting-point rule for markets, church and events.
Teach the Lost Plan to your brothers and sisters tonight.
discussion: Say the five Lost Plan steps in order.
Which helpers are safe in a market and which are not?
Why must you never wander around searching?
What should you agree with your parents before entering a busy place?
resources.assessment: Recitation of the Lost Plan and guardian data (or homework mission). Role-play performance observed.
resources.encouragement: You now carry a plan that even some grown-ups do not have! A lost child with a plan is found quickly; a lost child with the plan is a protected child. Memorise those numbers like your favourite song - they are gold. Ayekoo, my clever and safe children!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: My First Pocket Money
resources.why: Pocket money is a child's first taste of financial responsibility. Handled well, it teaches counting, keeping money safe, and the first taste of saving. Handled badly, it teaches waste and loss. Small money, big lessons.
outcomes: Count small Ghanaian coins and notes accurately.
Keep pocket money safe during the school day (fixed pocket or purse, counted before leaving home).
Decide spending with the simple question: do I need it or just want it?
Begin a simple saving habit with a home container and a small goal.
steps: Teacher displays real coins (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 pesewas; 1 and 2 cedis) and notes where relevant. Pupils identify and count sets aloud.
The safe-pocket rule: money goes in ONE fixed pocket or purse, zipped or buttoned; count it in the morning before leaving home; never flash it around - quiet money stays safe money.
Needs versus wants game: show picture cards (water, bread, toy car, biro, sweets, exercise book). Children sort: NEED or WANT? Discuss: needs first, wants later, sometimes never.
The daily plan: decide BEFORE school what the money is for (breakfast? bus fare? saving?). Money with no plan disappears by break time - money with a plan survives.
Introduce the save jar: an empty cleaned container at home with a slit and a label ('My Savings'). Agree a small goal (e.g., a storybook, a football) and a weekly amount, even 50 pesewas.
Practise a market scene: buying with correct change, counting change back, and saying thank you. Wrong change given? Count it before walking away.
Golden money rules recited: never take what is not given; never gamble or bet pocket money; never lend what you cannot lose quietly; tell parents if bigger money appears.
Home challenge: start the save jar this week; bring the counting story on Friday.
activities: Coin-counting relay in teams.
Needs-and-wants sorting race with picture cards.
Market role-play with real change counting.

reallife.situation: Kofi receives one cedi each morning, spends it all on sweets by 9 a.m., and then has nothing for the journey home.
reallife.way: Plan first: fare and food first, sweet last - and if there is anything left, it goes to the save jar, not sweets. The boy who plans his cedi today will manage thousands tomorrow.

reallife.situation: A child finds money in the classroom and keeps it quietly.
reallife.way: Found money goes to the teacher - the owner may be crying at home. Honest hands are trusted hands, and trusted hands are given bigger responsibilities and blessings.

home: Start a save jar with any amount, however small, this week.
Count your money each morning before school and keep it in one safe place.
Ask before spending: need or want?
discussion: Count these coins aloud as a class.
What is the difference between a need and a want? Give two examples of each.
Where does unplanned money usually go?
Why must quiet money stay quiet?
materials: Real or replica coins and notes
resources.assessment: Counting practical scored. Sorting game accuracy. Save-jar report Friday.
resources.encouragement: You are already money-wise at your young age - wonderful! Remember the golden order: needs first, wants later, savings always. The cedi you save today is a soldier fighting for your future. Keep your jar filling and your habits strong. Ayekoo, my little money masters!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: When I Make a Mistake: Say Sorry and Try Again
resources.why: Children who fear mistakes hide, lie or give up - and stop learning. Children who own mistakes, fix them and try again grow brave and wise. This lesson makes the classroom a safe place to fail, fix and fly.
outcomes: Admit a mistake honestly instead of hiding or blaming others.
Say a full, sincere apology: what I did, that it was wrong, and how I will fix it.
Fix what can be fixed (return, repair, replace, redo).
Try again after failing without shame or tears of defeat.
steps: Teacher shares a personal small mistake story (spilled the chalk water, wrote a wrong date on the board) and how it was fixed - modelling that even adults err.
Discuss the fear: why do children hide mistakes? (Scolding, shame, fear.) Agree together: in this class, honest mistakes are for learning; hiding them is the only real mistake.
Teach the Full Apology: 1) I did... 2) It was wrong because... 3) I am sorry. 4) I will fix it by... Practise in pairs with small scenes: broken pencil, torn book, pushed friend, forgotten homework.
Teach the Fix-it menu: return it, repair it, replace it, help the person, redo the work, or simply never repeat it.
Practise TRY AGAIN: teacher shows a wrong answer on the board, invites the class to find it, corrects it publicly with praise for the finder - normalising correction as celebration, not shame.
Handle feelings: a deep breath, 'mistakes teach me', stand tall and attempt again. Crying is allowed; quitting is not.
Discuss the lies trap: hiding a small mistake always grows a bigger trouble. Honesty clears the path quickly.
Class commitment: 'When I fall, I rise, I fix, I try again.' Every pupil says it aloud.
activities: Apology theatre: pairs perform the Full Apology in three scenes.
Fix-it menu game: match each mistake to its best fix.
Try-again chant with class rhythm; celebrate one publicly corrected error daily.

reallife.situation: A girl breaks mama's cup, hides it under the bed, and the blame falls on her little brother who is caned unjustly.
reallife.way: Own it the same hour: 'Mama, I broke the cup by accident, I am sorry, I will be careful next time.' A scolding ends in minutes; a lie poisons a home for days - and an innocent brother pays for it.

reallife.situation: A boy scores the lowest mark in class and announces he will never read again.
reallife.way: The comeback: find what went wrong, ask the teacher, practise that topic, try the next test. Falling is not failing - refusing to rise is. Every great person failed first and rose later.

home: Use the Full Apology once this week where it is truly needed.
Fix one small thing you spoiled (arrange it, repair it, replace it).
Retry one thing you gave up on - and report the comeback.
discussion: Say the four parts of the Full Apology.
Why does hiding a mistake make trouble grow?
What are four ways to fix a mistake?
What is the difference between falling and failing?
resources.assessment: Role-play of Full Apology scored on completeness and sincerity. Comeback reports shared and praised Friday.
resources.encouragement: Brave hearts! You have learned the most grown-up skill of all - admitting a mistake and rising stronger. Remember: the classroom is a training ground, and every error corrected here is a victory won. Fall seven times, stand up eight. Ayekoo, my courageous learners!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: My Morning Routine: Ready Before the Bell
resources.why: Late arrivals steal learning and bring shame. Children who own a fixed morning routine - wake, clean, eat, dress, move - arrive early, calm and ready. A peaceful morning is built the night before, and it is a habit any child can master.
outcomes: Build and follow a personal morning routine chart from wake-up to school gate.
Complete hygiene, dressing, breakfast and bag-check steps in the right order.
Estimate time needed and wake early enough to avoid rushing.
Prepare the night before (bag packed, uniform ready) to make mornings easy.
steps: Teacher draws two mornings on the board: the rushing morning (late, no breakfast, dirty uniform, tears) and the winning morning (early, calm, ready). Class chooses which life they want.

Build the routine chart together, in order: 1) Wake when called (or by alarm) - no three-times calling. 2) Face and hands, bath with soap. 3) Brush teeth. 4) Dress in the uniform that was laid out LAST NIGHT. 5) Eat breakfast - the brain's fuel for morning lessons. 6) Final bag check against the checklist (LS-LP-001). 7) Greet and bless the house. 8) Leave early enough to arrive with time to spare.
Night-before habits demonstrated: bag packed, uniform folded on a chair, shoes cleaned and placed at the door - so morning is half done before sleep.
Time-talk: how long does each step take? Children estimate; teacher adds. The total shows why 'I woke late' is really 'I woke at the wrong time'.
Practice recitation: each pupil says their own routine aloud with times ('I wake at 5:30, bath, dress, eat at 6:00...').
The greeting habit: leaving home with a greeting and blessing ('I am going to school' to parents) - respect travels with readiness.
Set the class challenge: seven early-and-complete mornings, ticked by a parent on the routine chart.
Friday celebration: early birds share how their calm mornings changed their lessons.
activities: Routine puzzle: mixed step-cards ordered correctly against a clock.
Draw-my-morning poster for home display.
Night-before relay: pack bag, lay uniform, place shoes - performed as a race.

reallife.situation: Every morning is war: Adjoa wakes with the second or third call, hunts for her uniform, skips breakfast, and reaches school after the first lesson has started.
reallife.way: The fix is mostly the NIGHT before: bag packed, uniform ready, shoes waiting. Then wake earlier, follow the order, and breakfast happens. Seven mornings of discipline turn the war into a walk.

reallife.situation: A boy arrives late twice in a week and misses the mathematics topics that later appear in his test.
reallife.way: Late arrival steals tomorrow's marks. Fix the routine and even the difficult subject becomes learnable, because you were in the room when it was taught.

home: Create and tick your routine chart every morning for one week.
Prepare the night before: bag, uniform, shoes.
Report your first calm-morning experience on Friday.
discussion: Recite your morning routine with times.
Why is the night before the secret of a good morning?
What does arriving early give you that arriving late takes away?
Whose job is your morning - the alarm's, mama's, or yours?
resources.assessment: Seven-day chart returned. Routine recitation observed. Participation in ordering game.
resources.encouragement: Champions rise early and arrive ready - and now that is YOU! A calm morning gives you a strong lesson, and strong lessons give you a strong future. Set that routine ticking from tonight. I believe in every one of you. Ayekoo, my punctual champions!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Washing Clothes by Hand, Step by Step
resources.why: Almost every Ghanaian household washes clothes by hand, yet most children are never taught the proper order - so clothes tear, colours run, and washing takes twice as long. A child who masters the steps does the work faster, protects the fabric, and carries a skill for life.
outcomes: Sort clothes before washing: whites, colours, heavily soiled; check pockets first.
Wash a garment by hand through the full cycle: soak, soap, scrub, knead, rinse twice, wring.
Dry clothes properly on the line: shake, spread, pin or drape correctly, turn inside out for coloured fabrics.
Explain why each step protects either the clothes or the skin.
steps: Teacher displays three garments (school shirt, coloured dress, white socks) and asks: what can go wrong if we wash them all together? Discussion: colour bleeding, spreading dirt.
STEP 1 - Inspect and sort: empty all pockets (pens ruin shirts, money is lost), close zips, sort whites, colours and very dirty items into separate piles.
STEP 2 - Soak: soak very dirty items briefly in water with a little soap; whites separately from colours.
STEP 3 - Soap and scrub: apply soap on collar, cuffs, underarm and hem zones; scrub on a clean surface or between palms with moderate force - scrubbing hard on thin fabric tears it.
STEP 4 - Knead and wring: squeeze and knead the garment like dough so soap lifts dirt; wring gently for delicate items, firmly for sturdy ones.
STEP 5 - Rinse twice: first rinse removes soap, second rinse confirms it - water must run clear; leftover soap irritates skin and dulls fabric.
STEP 6 - Line discipline: shake each item hard (removes wrinkles and lint), spread fully with no folded-over edges, pin or drape properly; colours dry inside-out in shade; whites love full sun.
STEP 7 - When dry: fold immediately (link to LS-LP-004 habit) or iron if available. Teacher recapitulates the chant: 'Sort, soak, scrub, knead, rinse twice, spread, fold.'
Group practice at water source with supervision; each pupil washes and displays one item; class judges with a checklist: no soap left, no tears, spread well.
activities: Full-cycle practice: each group washes one shirt from sort to fold.
Checklist inspection relay: teams inspect rivals' drying technique.
Stain strategy discussion: mud, oil and ink - pre-soak, target soap, patience.

reallife.situation: A boy washes his red shirt together with white shirts and by afternoon all the whites have turned pink.
reallife.way: Sort before you soak - colours with colours, whites alone. A red garment bleeding is normal; the disaster is mixing. Sorting takes one minute; re-dyeing whites costs more than a week's washing effort.

reallife.situation: A girl scrubs her uniform so violently that the elbows tear within a month and mama complains about buying new ones.
reallife.way: Work smart: let soap and soaking do the work, not brute force. Target the dirty zones with firm but gentle strokes. Clothes that last two years save the family real money.

home: Wash your own clothes this week through the full seven steps.
Rinse twice and dry properly - no soap left, no folded-over wet edges.
Fold or iron immediately when dry.
discussion: Recite the washing chant in order.
Why do colours and whites never share a soak?
Why must soap be rinsed out completely?
Why dry coloured clothes inside-out in the shade?
resources.assessment: Practical: wash one garment through all steps; scored on order, care and result. Oral: the chant and two reasons for sorting.
resources.encouragement: Look at your hands - they have learned a skill millions of families rely on daily! You can now wash smarter, faster and kinder to the fabric. Keep the chant, keep the standard, and your clothes will always be ready and your hands always trusted. Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Setting the Table and Serving at Home
resources.why: Meals are the family's daily meeting, and a child who sets a clean table, serves elders in the right order and clears properly is a treasure in any home. These small courtesies - serving elders first, holding bowls correctly, clearing and cleaning after - carry deep Ghanaian respect.
outcomes: Set a proper eating place: clean surface, mat if available, bowls, cups and spoons arranged neatly.
Serve respectfully: wash hands first, elders first, no leaning over food, no fingers in serving bowls.
Carry and clear dishes safely and quietly.
Show mealtime manners: greeting, thank you after the meal, and helping to clear.
steps: Teacher asks: who serves food at home? Children share experiences; teacher honours the role.

Demonstrate setting: wipe the surface or spread the mat; place bowls and spoons neatly aligned for each person; water in clean cups; serving spoons on a clean saucer beside the pot - never inside the food.
Demonstrate serving order: wash your own hands first, serve the eldest first, then down the line; children eat after adults are served; no serving bowl is touched with fingers or personal spoon.
Carrying practice: bowl with two hands, held steady, eyes on the path; hot bowls are carried only by adults or with permission; walk slowly, no running.
Clearing demonstration: gather all dishes to one station, scrape leftovers into the bin or a bowl for animals (with adult's direction), stack cups inside bowls, carry out in one smart trip.
After-meal manners: 'Thank you for the food, Mama' to the cook; wipe the table, sweep the crumbs, cover the remaining food properly (link to LS-UP-003).
Role-play circuit: a family dinner scene - one child sets, one serves, guests greet, the youngest clears; rotate so everyone plays every role.
Discuss special guests at the table: greet them, serve them first, do not stare or snatch; the table is where a family's training shows most.
activities: Table-setting race with judged neatness (alignment beats speed).
Serving order drill: arrange pictures of family members in serving order.
Full meal role-play: set, greet, serve, eat with manners, clear, clean, thank.

reallife.situation: A child serves food leaning across the pot, drops rice on the floor, and uses his personal spoon in the shared bowl - guests exchange looks.
reallife.way: Serve standing steady, one clean serving spoon per dish, elders first. At the Ghanaian table, technique is respect: the way a child serves tells the guests how that child was raised.

reallife.situation: After dinner, plates are left for morning and flies feast overnight; the kitchen smells by dawn.
reallife.way: Clear, scrape, wash or at least rinse and cover - same night, every night. The child who clears the table finishes the meal with honour; the kitchen sleeps clean.

home: Set the table and serve your family at least twice this week.
Serve elders first and thank the cook after the meal.
Clear and wipe the table without being told.
discussion: Describe a properly set eating place.
Who is served first and why?
Why must the serving spoon never be your personal spoon?
What do you do after the meal besides eating?
resources.assessment: Practical table-setting judged. Role-play observed on serving order, carrying and clearing.
resources.encouragement: What fine table officers you have become! Guests will bless your families because of the way you serve and clear. Remember: the child who serves with skill and honour is trusted with bigger responsibilities. Keep the table beautiful and the manners shining. Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Keeping Food Safe at Home
resources.why: Food waste and food poisoning often begin with simple mistakes: uncovered leftovers, unkempt storage, ignoring smell and expiry. Children who know how to store, cover and test food protect their family's health and the family's money at the same time.
outcomes: Store cooked food safely: cover, elevate, cool place or fridge where available.
Apply the smell, look and date checks before eating or serving stored food.
Explain how flies, ants, rats and moisture spoil food and how each is blocked.
Reduce food waste at home with smart storage and reheating.
steps: Teacher displays three samples (safely simulated): uncovered rice, covered rice, spoiled soup. Class discusses which is safe and why we can be tricked by appearance.

Storage rules built with the class: 1) Cool hot food briefly, then cover it well. 2) Store on an elevated rack or in the fridge - floor storage invites ants, rats and moisture. 3) Use clean, dry containers with tight lids. 4) Keep raw foods away from cooked foods; separate cutting surfaces where possible.

The three checks before serving stored food: SMELL (sour or off = do not eat), LOOK (mould, strange colour, watery film = do not eat), DATE (how many days? 'yesterday's stew' rules vary - when unsure, ask an adult).
Reheating wisdom: warm food thoroughly (steaming hot) before serving - lukewarm reheating protects germs, not people.

The enemies game: flies (carry germs from gutters to food), ants (contaminate and annoy), rats (spread disease), moisture (breeds mould). For each enemy, the class proposes the block: tight lids, clean surfaces, sealed containers, dry storage.
Dry-goods talk: gari, rice, beans and flour live in sealed, dry containers; a spoonful of moisture ruins a bag; inspect and sun-dry grains where the family does this.
Discuss wasting less: serve what will be eaten, finish plates or store leftovers immediately, rotate older food to the front.
Home challenge: audit your family's food storage - find three uncovered foods and propose covers or containers; report on Friday.
activities: Safe-or-spoiled decision cards based on smell, look and date.
Enemy-and-block matching game.
Kitchen audit drawing: mark safe and risky storage spots in a kitchen picture.

reallife.situation: A family eats stew left uncovered overnight; by evening several are vomiting - a hospital visit follows.
reallife.way: Uncovered food is an open invitation to flies and germs; the poison is invisible until the body complains. Cover everything, cool and elevate it, and when in doubt about smell or age - throw it out rather than gamble with health.

reallife.situation: Bags of gari and beans sit open in the storeroom; ants march in and moisture caking sets in, and much is thrown away.
reallife.way: Sealed, dry containers turn losses into savings. Food kept well is money kept well - a small plastic lid protects a whole week's budget.

home: Audit your kitchen: list uncovered or floor-stored foods and suggest fixes.
Practise the three checks (smell, look, date) before eating stored food this week.
Propose one storage improvement to your family and try it.
discussion: Name the three checks before serving stored food.
Which four enemies spoil food, and how do we block each?
Why is lukewarm reheated food dangerous?
How does smart storage save the family money?
resources.assessment: Decision-card game scored. Home audit report assessed. Oral: the three checks and two storage rules.
resources.encouragement: You are now the family's food guardian! Every covered pot and smart check you make protects lives and pockets. Behind many hospital visits is a simple storage mistake - and you know how to prevent it. Practise your checks until they are automatic. Ayekoo, wise keepers!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Sewing: Buttons, Tears and the Home Mending Kit
resources.why: A torn shirt does not need a tailor - it needs twenty minutes and a threaded needle. Children who can sew a button, close a small tear and keep a mending kit save clothes, save money and stand out among their peers as truly capable.
outcomes: Thread a needle, knot the end and sew a button securely with a few firm stitches.
Close a straight tear with a simple running stitch.
Assemble and maintain a home mending kit: needle, thread in common colours, small scissors, spare buttons, pins.
Explain how mending skills save money and extend the life of clothes.
steps: Teacher displays a shirt missing a button and one with a small tear. Ask: throw it away or fix it? Class discusses money and waste.
Needle safety rules first: needles sit in the pincushion or kit, never in the mouth, collar or sofa; pass needles handle-first; count your needles before and after work.
Threading demonstration: moisten the thread end, push it through the eye, pull a comfortable length, knot the far end with a double knot. Pupils practise threading until each succeeds.
Button demo: position the button, anchor the thread from behind, pass through button holes and fabric 4-6 times, end with a hidden knot at the back, trim.
Tear demo: match the edges, start just before the tear, running stitch (small, even, forward-back), finish with a knot; compare a stitched tear with a pinned-and-forgotten one.

Build the Home Mending Kit on the table: container, needles, threads in common colours (black, white, brown, navy), small scissors, spare buttons, pins, tape measure optional. Each pupil lists what their home kit needs.
Practice stations: everyone sews one button and closes one tear; slow, careful, counted stitches; teacher checks firmness by a gentle pull.
Home challenge: mend one garment this week and set up the family kit; report the mend on Friday.
activities: Threading relay: first team with all threads through wins, but only with safe needle handling.
Button-and-tear workshop: each pupil completes one of each.
Kit inventory exercise: list and cost (in cedis) the kit items and compare with the cost of one new shirt.

reallife.situation: A pupil's shirt button pops during assembly every week and the teacher keeps calling out his untucked look - the shirt eventually sits unused.
reallife.way: Four minutes with needle and thread ends the problem permanently. A button is a two-minute fix; neglecting it costs a whole uniform. Fix-it skills make a child independent.

reallife.situation: A family discards clothes for small tears and spends heavily on new ones every term.
reallife.way: A mending kit under fifty cedis can serve a family for years. One evening of mending restores several garments. Children who mend become adults who save.

home: Sew one button and close one tear this week.
Assemble or list a home mending kit for your family.
Report your mend on Friday and show the garment.
discussion: Demonstrate threading and knotting for the class.
Recite the needle safety rules.
How does a mending kit save a family money?
Which stitches hold a button firmly - few loose or several firm?
resources.assessment: Practical: one button and one tear sewn; firmness tested gently. Kit list assessed for completeness.
resources.encouragement: Masterful fingers! You now hold a skill that clothes, bags, and even your future households will thank you for. A child who can mend is a child who wastes nothing - and waste-nothing people always prosper. Keep your kit ready and your stitches neat. Ayekoo!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Cleaning the Home Like a Professional
resources.why: Cleaning a whole home is different from sweeping a room: it needs a plan, an order, and the right motion for each surface. Children who learn the professional way - top to bottom, back to front, dust before wet - finish faster with better results and less back-aching repetition.
outcomes: Plan a room cleaning in the professional order: tidy, dust, sweep, mop/wipe, air.
Apply the top-to-bottom, back-to-front rule and explain why.
Clean windows, shelves and a bathroom area safely and thoroughly.
Divide home cleaning among family members fairly and quickly.
steps: Teacher poses the problem: why does a child who sweeps for an hour still have a dusty room? Discussion reveals the missing system.

The Pro Order: 1) TIDY - clothes to the basket, books to the shelf, items to their homes (dust hides under clutter). 2) DUST - top to bottom (shelf, frame, table edges, skirting), dust falls to the floor, never the reverse. 3) SWEEP - corners to centre, under furniture where reachable. 4) WET CLEAN - mop or wipe the floor, wipe surfaces with a damp cloth; bucket water changed when dirty. 5) AIR - open windows, let the room breathe; smell is the final proof.

Technique demonstrations: the figure-8 damp-mop motion for floors; straight strokes on windows in one direction (strokes crossing = streaks); squeezing cloths properly so surfaces are wiped, not flooded.
Bathroom basics: Ventilation, then scrub bowl and floor last so dirt travels downward, always; rinse buckets; never mix cleaning chemicals.

Working smart: bucket and materials gathered BEFORE starting (one trip, not twenty); doors and windows cleaned on different days from deep floors; a fifteen-minute daily tidy beats a three-hour weekend war.
Team chore chart: the class designs a fair family rota (kitchen, compound, rooms, bathroom) with realistic daily minutes; fairness is discussed - small children get lighter tasks but are not excused.
Practice circuit: corners of the classroom or school veranda cleaned by teams using the Pro Order; judge: spotless corners, no water flooding, time used.
Home challenge: clean one full room or area this week using the Pro Order and report the difference.
activities: Pro-order card race: teams arrange mixed cleaning steps correctly.
Mop-motion clinic on a marked floor square.
Design-a-rota workshop with fairness scoring.

reallife.situation: A child mops first, then sweeps, then dusts the high shelf - by evening the floor shows dust lines again and the work must be repeated.
reallife.way: The order is the work: dust falls downward, so it comes before the wet clean. Doing the sequence right once beats doing it wrong three times. Work smart, not merely hard.

reallife.situation: One child does all the cleaning alone every weekend while others watch, and resentment grows at home.
reallife.way: A rota makes cleaning a family team sport: everyone owns a zone, small hands take small tasks. Fairness keeps peace; skills rotate so every child learns every corner of the home.

home: Clean one full room or area this week in the professional order.
Gather all materials before you start - the one-trip rule.
Propose a fair family rota and report on it Friday.
discussion: Recite the Pro Order with reasons for each step.
Why dust before sweeping, and sweep before mopping?
What does the one-trip rule save you?
How is a fair rota designed?
resources.assessment: Practical cleaning of a marked area scored on order and finish. Rota assessed for fairness. Oral: the Pro Order.
resources.encouragement: Professional hands, well done! You have learned that smart work beats sweaty work - plan the order, gather the tools, finish once, finish well. The homes you will keep someday will sparkle because of today. Ayekoo, my hardworking professionals!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Fetching and Storing Water Safely
resources.why: Water fetching is daily reality in many Ghanaian homes, and it carries real risks: accidents on the head from overfilling, contaminated storage, and wasted trips from poor planning. Doing it safely and smartly protects the body and the family's most precious resource.
outcomes: Fetch water safely: balanced container, sensible fill level, careful path choice, no running.
Store water safely: covered, elevated, clean containers; drinking water separated from washing water.
Practise hygiene around water points: dirty containers, hands and cups re-contaminate clean water.
Use water wisely: no waste while fetching, washing or cleaning.
steps: Teacher asks: how is water fetched and stored at home? Compile the current practice; identify risks together.

Fetching rules: fill to a sensible level (a container brimming over the head is an accident waiting); check the handle or lid; watch the path for stones, mud and traffic; walk, never run; older children help younger ones.
The balance trick: distribute weight evenly, switch sides or use both hands on long trips, rest the container on a raised surface instead of the ground when pausing.

Storage rules: use clean containers washed regularly; keep them COVERED always - uncovered water invites dust, insects, lizards and disease; store on a stand or rack, not the bare floor; use a clean scoop kept only for that container.
Separation rule: drinking water is kept apart from washing water; when the source is untreated, drinking water is boiled, filtered or treated per adult guidance, and stored distinctly.
Water wisdom: a closed tap or tightened tap saves litres; wash with a bowl rather than under a running stream where water is scarce; report leaking taps and broken pipes to adults quickly.
Discuss the journey: long water walks cost time and school minutes - fetch in fewer, fuller (but safe) trips planned around school hours.
Home challenge: fetch and store water safely this week; inspect your home's containers and report what you improved.
activities: Balance practice: containers filled to safe levels, carried along a marked path.
Storage inspection role-play: find the mistakes in a picture of a home water point.
Water-saving pledge posters for home taps.

reallife.situation: A girl overfills her basin, water sloshes onto the path, and she slips and injures her arm - the water is lost too.
reallife.way: Fill below the brim, mind the path, walk steady. Speed is false economy; one fall costs more than ten careful trips.

reallife.situation: The family's drinking pot stands open with a shared cup dropped inside; children dip fingers and cups directly.
reallife.way: Covered pot, raised stand, clean scoop, no dipping. Clean water protected stays clean; a single dirty hand at the mouth of the pot can undo a whole day's fetching.

home: Practise safe fetching: sensible fill, steady walk, safe path.
Check and improve home water containers: covered, raised, clean scoop.
Report one leak or waste you spotted and stopped.
discussion: Why is an overfilled container dangerous?
Recite the storage rules for drinking water.
Why keep drinking water separate from washing water?
How can a family waste less water daily?
resources.assessment: Balance walk observed. Storage audit report assessed. Oral: two storage rules and one safety rule.
resources.encouragement: Strong and wise - that is the water carrier's way! You now protect both the body and the water itself: steady hands, covered pots, clean scoops. Water is life, and today you learned to handle life with care. Ayekoo, faithful carriers!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: My Savings Plan: Save Some, Spend Some, Help Some
resources.why: Money that arrives without a plan vanishes without a trace. The save-some-spend-some-help-some rule turns any amount - even coins - into three useful streams: a growing future, a happy present, and a generous heart. This is the habit behind every financially stable adult.
outcomes: Divide money into three parts: savings, spending and helping/giving, with a fixed ratio.
Set a savings goal with a target amount, date and plan.
Track savings weekly and celebrate milestones honestly.
Explain why saving first and spending after beats the opposite.
steps: Teacher tells the story of two pupils with equal weekly money: one spends-first, one saves-first. Where are they in three months? Class calculates.
The Three-Jar rule: JAR 1 SAVE (at least 1 of every 10, more if possible), JAR 2 SPEND (planned needs and honest treats), JAR 3 HELP (gifts, offerings, family needs, the classmate in real trouble).
Set a personal goal: what exactly (a dictionary, football, bicycle), how much, by when. Write it: 'By [date] I will have [amount] saved for [goal].' Post it where the money container lives.
Weekly maths practice: money received minus planned division = jars filled; small class sums with real numbers so the plan becomes arithmetic, not speeches.
Defend the savings jar from yourself: it lives out of easy reach, it has a slit so money goes in but temptation does not come out, and dipping requires a written reason agreed with an adult.
The help jar discussion: our culture is communal - the jar teaches generosity with a plan (offering, a sibling's pencil, mother's sachet water money), never forced, always from the heart.
Track on a savings record: date, amount in, total, goal remaining. Watching the total climb is the quiet joy of the disciplined.
Home challenge: create the three containers this week with a parent's blessing; make the first deposit and record it.
activities: Three-jar setup workshop with labelled containers.
Goal-setting sheet: goal, amount, date, weekly plan - displayed at home.
Weekly sums: divide example amounts into the three jars and fill a savings record.

reallife.situation: Akua receives money daily, spends-first, and by month's end cannot buy even the exercise book she needed.
reallife.way: Save first, spend after - the jar discipline reverses the ending. The exercise book appears in month two, bought by her own patience. Small order, big results.

reallife.situation: A boy saves faithfully but dips into his jar every week for snacks and never reaches the target.
reallife.way: Put the jar out of reach, agree dipping rules with an adult, and record every deposit. The record itself discourages dipping - nobody enjoys erasing progress.

home: Set up three jars or envelopes with your family's blessing this week.
Write and post a savings goal with amount and date.
Make at least two deposits and show the record Friday.
discussion: State the three-jar rule and a sensible ratio.
Why does save-first beat spend-first? Show with a small calculation.
What makes dipping into savings less likely?
Why include a help jar at all?
resources.assessment: Jars set up and first deposits recorded. Weekly sums accuracy. Friday record reviewed.
resources.encouragement: Three jars and a dream - you are building a financial future already! The person who controls small money today will stand firm before big money tomorrow. Keep the jars filling, the records honest, and the goal in sight. Ayekoo, my wise savers!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Needs Come Before Wants
resources.why: The market is full of shouting temptations, and a child without the needs-first compass buys today and regrets tonight. Distinguishing needs from wants - and honouring needs first - is the seed of every budget, every savings plan and every stable home.
outcomes: Sort spending items confidently into needs and wants with reasons.
Rank a mixed list by importance when money is limited.
Practise postponing wants: the wait-and-save rule.
Explain how needs-first thinking protects a family in hard times.
steps: Teacher writes a market list with mixed items: exercise books, sweets, soap, toy gun, fare, biscuit, slippers, football. Money available is limited - class must rank the list.

Define the two clearly: NEEDS keep us healthy, learning and moving (food, books, soap, fare); WANTS make life sweet but can wait (toys, extra sweets, games). Some items sit between - discuss honestly (a football for exercise and team spirit?).
Sorting relay with picture cards; disputed cards go to class debate with reasons - the point is reasoning, not memorising.
The limited-money drill: give a fixed amount and a mixed list; teams must buy needs fully first and justify every want they keep.
Teach the wait-and-save rule: a want postponed while saving grows usually arrives better - bought with your own saved money, chosen wisely, treasured longer.
Discuss family reality: parents also rank needs before wants; understanding this makes children easier to live with and grateful for every want that is met.
Hard-times talk: in lean months, families cut wants first, then some needs get clever substitutes; children who understand this do not sulk - they help.
Home challenge: rank your own wish list this week - needs first, wants later - and discuss it with a parent.
activities: Card-sorting relay with disputed-card debate.
Fixed-budget team shopping drill with justification.
Personal wish list ranking for home discussion.

reallife.situation: A boy spends his whole week's money on a toy gun and then has no money for fare and exercises; he borrows and falls into small debts.
reallife.way: Needs first, always. Fare and books come before toys; the toy waits while savings grow. The borrower becomes the beggar - and the planner becomes the buyer.

reallife.situation: A girl sulks because her friend's parents bought new sandals and hers are old.
reallife.way: Old sandals polished and cared for beat new sandals worn carelessly. Gratitude turns what we have into enough; comparison turns plenty into poverty of the heart.

home: Rank your wish list: needs first, wants after, with reasons.
Practise wait-and-save on one small want this week.
Discuss the list with a parent and report Friday.
discussion: Define needs and wants with two examples each.
Rank this mixed list and defend your order.
What does wait-and-save achieve?
Why do parents sometimes say no even when money exists?
resources.assessment: Sorting accuracy with reasoning. Ranking drill performance. Home discussion report.
resources.encouragement: You have gained the marketer's sharpest eye - the needs-first lens! With it, no crowd of temptations can mislead you. Practise the ranking this week and feel the power of a clear head at the market. Ayekoo, my wise shoppers!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Money and Honesty: It Is Not Mine Until It Is Given
resources.why: Money tests character more than anything else in a child's world: a coin on the teacher's table, change at the market, a purse left in the classroom. Children who pass these tests build a name that opens every future door - children who fail begin a path that hardens with age.
outcomes: State the rule: money and items are not mine until they are given to me - even if found, even if unwatched.
Return found money and items through the proper channel (teacher, owner, adult).
Count and return correct change; report wrong change honestly.
Ask before borrowing and repay promptly; never 'borrow' without permission.
steps: Teacher sets three tempting scenes (acted or described): a fifty-cedi note on the classroom floor; extra change given at the shop; a classmate's purse visible in an unattended bag.
Class debates each: 'finders keepers' versus honesty. Guide to the hard truth: every note belongs to somebody - often somebody who worked hard for it and is suffering at that very moment.

The found-money protocol: pick it up openly (so it is not lost again), hand it to the teacher or the nearest adult, and let it be announced. The finder who reports gets honour; the finder who hides builds a hidden self.
Change honesty: count your change before leaving the seller; extra change returned brings blessing and builds your market name; keeping silent change steals from a person, not from a shop.
Borrowing rules: ask first, name the day of return, repay on that day; borrowing without asking is taking. If you cannot repay, say so early and face it - never dodge.
Discuss the slippery slope: small dishonesties with money grow into big ones - the child who keeps one coin today faces harder tests tomorrow with a trained hand.
Character maths: money lost to honesty is small and temporary; trust lost to dishonesty is large and long. Write the equation on the board.
Home challenge: one honest-money act this week (return something, report change, repay a debt) and report it Friday.
activities: Honesty role-plays: the found note, the extra change, the visible purse - each with the correct protocol performed.
Character equation poster: money lost vs trust lost.
Repayment calendar exercise: plan the return of a small borrowed amount.

reallife.situation: A boy finds a folded note in the classroom, pockets it silently, and spends it on sweets - while a classmate searches everywhere crying, because that was her fare for the whole week.
reallife.way: Hand it to the teacher the moment you find it. The tears you prevent are worth more than the note; the name you build is worth more than both.

reallife.situation: A pupil borrows a friend's two cedis 'just for today' and avoids the friend for a month.
reallife.way: Debt dodged becomes friendship buried. Repay or speak early: 'Brother, I cannot pay yet - give me until Friday.' A debtor who talks keeps his friend; one who hides loses both money and name.

home: Perform one honest-money act this week and report it.
Repay any small debt you owe, or speak about it honestly.
Teach the found-money protocol to a sibling.
discussion: What is the protocol for found money?
Why is extra change a test and not a gift?
State the borrowing rules.
How do small dishonesties grow?
resources.assessment: Role-play protocol performed correctly. Friday honesty report. Oral: the character equation.
resources.encouragement: You have chosen the richer path - honest hands and a clean name! Money comes and goes, but a trusted name gathers friends, opportunities and blessing for a lifetime. Keep your hands clean and your words true. Ayekoo, my honest ones!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: My Weekly Timetable: Study, Play, Rest, Help
resources.why: Children who drift through the week end it with unfinished homework, missed chores and no rest. A simple weekly timetable - with study blocks, play, chores and rest clearly marked - gives every day a shape and removes the daily argument about what to do next.
outcomes: Design a personal weekly timetable balancing study, play, chores, rest and family time.
Place the hardest study task at the best personal time (not always the latest hour).
Follow the timetable for one week with ticks and honest notes.
Adjust the timetable when it fails, instead of abandoning it.
steps: Teacher displays a blank week grid (Monday-Sunday, morning-afternoon-evening blocks) and asks: what MUST appear every week? Class lists: school, homework, study, chores, play, rest, worship/family time, sleep.

Discuss the study golden hour: each child has a time when the brain is freshest (some early morning, some right after school, some evening). The hardest subject gets the golden hour - not the leftover scraps of the day.

Fill the grid in pencil: fixed items first (school, church/mosque, family duties), then study blocks with subjects named, then play and rest. Play is a scheduled citizen, not an intruder - a timetable without play is abandoned in a week.
Chores placement: link to the home (fetching water, cleaning, kitchen help) so the timetable serves the family, not just the pupil.
The tick system: each completed block gets a tick; each missed block gets a one-line reason. Friday review: count ticks, read reasons, adjust next week.

Adjustment philosophy taught: a timetable is a servant, not a god. If Thursday evening always fails, move the block; if a subject needs more time, take it from a lighter one. Failing blocks are data, not disgrace.
Sleep is protected: fixed bedtime and wake time; a tired brain cannot study and cannot play well either.
Home challenge: run your timetable for seven days with a parent's signature on the Friday review.
activities: Timetable design workshop on personal grids.
Golden-hour quiz: each pupil states their best study hour and defends it.
Friday review clinic: trade timetables, peer-check honesty of ticks.

reallife.situation: Yaw 'plans to study after dinner' every day, but by evening he is tired, the TV is on, and homework sleeps unfinished - a pattern repeating all term.
