What if it is at home? Some students face pressure from relatives or older neighbours - reporting still applies: teacher, school counsellor, or a trusted adult; silence feeds the habit.
Helping a friend already in it: no mocking, no joining, no secrecy when danger grows - tell a trusted adult; the friend may be angry today and alive tomorrow.
The identity anchor: write your own one-line identity ('I am going to...') - refusals are easier when the destination is written.
Home challenge: rehearse all three scripts aloud until they are yours; write your identity line; report (privately, if needed) any pressure you are facing.
activities: Refusal drill circuit: three scripts against staged pressure with feedback.
Offer-decoding exercise on real pressure lines.
Identity-anchor writing session.

reallife.situation: At a birthday party, older boys pass a bottle and laughter surrounds any refusal.
reallife.way: Plain no, steady eyes, exit early with the friends who share your plans. The bottle's friendship lasts a night; your brain's friendship lasts a lifetime.

reallife.situation: A student notices his best friend returning to school smelling of wee and changing fast.
reallife.way: Do not mock, do not join, do not keep the dangerous secret: tell a trusted adult early. Friends pulled early are friends saved; friends reported late are friends buried.

home: Rehearse the three refusal scripts aloud until natural.
Write your identity line and keep it visible.
Report any pressure you face to a trusted adult - privately is fine.
discussion: Decode the four pressure lines.
Perform the plain-no and exit scripts.
What do you do for a friend already trapped?
Why is 'just once' rarely just once?
resources.assessment: Refusal drill performance. Offer decoding accuracy. Identity line quality.
resources.encouragement: You now carry scripts stronger than any pressure! The power to refuse is real power - quiet, firm and free. Rehearse until the no is automatic, keep your circle clean, and walk towards those BECE plans. Ayekoo, my strong refusers!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Tramadol and 'Enhancers': The Truth That Saves Lives
resources.why: Among JHS students, tramadol and similar pills are marketed in whispers as strength for labour, stamina for night study, courage for peers, or an escape from pain. The truth: they poison the growing brain, trap users fast, and have destroyed scores of young Ghanaians. Straight talk saves.
outcomes: State the real effects of tramadol and similar pills on the adolescent brain, body and future.
Expose the marketing myths: strength, stamina, boldness, escape, 'medicinal' cover.
Identify the trap cycle: first pill, tolerance, dependence, and the road out through help.
Know the helping routes for oneself and for friends - and use them early.
steps: Facts first, plainly: tramadol is a strong painkiller meant for real medical need, prescribed and controlled; misused, it hijacks the brain's chemistry - first tolerance (more needed for the same effect), then dependence, then a life arranged around the pill.

The five myths dismantled: 'it gives strength' (it borrows from your future and repays weakness); 'it keeps you awake to study' (it wrecks the memory you are studying to build); 'it makes you brave' (it numbs judgement - the opposite of courage); 'it is medicine, so it is safe' (medicine in the right dose for the right reason; stolen strength is poison); 'everybody does it' (the graveyard of that argument is full).

The trap cycle taught openly: how the first 'just one to see' becomes a need the user never planned; how sellers target students at their weakest hours; how the cycle ends for those who do not exit - and how it ends well for those who do.

The exit route: telling a trusted adult early is not weakness - it is the strongest move on the board. School counsellor, teacher, parent, or a health worker; the earlier the telling, the easier the rescue.

For friends: the signs (sudden cash hunger, new secretive friends, red eyes, falling grades,缺席 from home); the duty - do not mock, do not join, do not keep the dangerous secret; tell early. Friendship that reports saves; friendship that hides buries.

Pain and pressure addressed honestly: students carrying grief, fear or family pain are targets - the healthy routes (talking to trusted adults, school support, faith, sport) deliver what the pill only borrows.
The identity anchor reused: students who know where they are going find pills a poor vehicle; write the line again if it has faded.
Home challenge: know the signs, know the route, and - where it touches you or a friend - take the strong step this week: tell a trusted adult.
activities: Myth-dismantling workshop: groups defeat each myth with the truth.
Signs-and-route role-play: recognising a friend in the trap and choosing the helping move.
Identity anchor redrafting session.

reallife.situation: Labourer boys introduce a student to tramadol 'for energy' on a holiday work stint; within months his memory and money are both gone.
reallife.way: Strength borrowed from pills is repaid with interest by the brain. The exit is early truth-telling to a trusted adult - the road back is real, and it begins with a single honest conversation.

reallife.situation: A girl grieving a family loss is offered pills 'to feel better' by a schoolmate's older brother.
reallife.way: Grief needs comfort, company and time - not chemistry. Tell the trusted adult the same day; the pill's comfort is a loan shark: it collects your tomorrow.

home: Memorise the signs and the helping route.
Tell a trusted adult about any pressure touching you or a friend - this week, if it exists.
Redraft your identity line if it has faded.
discussion: Dismantle the five myths with the truth.
List the warning signs in a friend.
Why is early telling the strongest move?
What does a growing brain lose to the pill?
resources.assessment: Myth-dismantling quality. Signs-and-route role-play. Identity anchor review.
resources.encouragement: Truth-carriers, stand firm! You now know what the whisperers hope you never learn - and knowing is protection. Keep your brain, guard your friends, use the strong route of truth-telling early. There is no shortcut worth your tomorrow. Ayekoo, my wise ones!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Unwanted Advances: No Is a Complete Answer
resources.why: Adolescence attracts attention that is not always safe: gifts with hooks, 'special friendship' talk from older people, touches that make the skin crawl. Students must hear it plainly: your body is yours, no is a complete sentence, and telling trusted adults about pressure is protection - never disgrace.
outcomes: Recognise unsafe attention: secret gifts, private-meeting invitations, touch that discomforts, pressure dressed as love.
Refuse clearly and leave: firm no, distance, safe routes, trusted company.
Report pressure to trusted adults early and understand that the fault belongs to the pressurer, never the child.
Protect friends: notice changes, offer company, encourage telling.
steps: The foundation said plainly and without embarrassment: your body belongs to you; nobody - however old, however generous, however related - has a right to touch you or pressure you; a secret asked to be kept is already a warning bell.

The lures exposed: sudden gifts or money from an older 'admirer'; requests to meet in private places or odd hours; 'do not tell anyone, this is our secret'; touch or talk that makes the skin uneasy. Unease is information - trust it.

Refusal and exit drilled: the firm no ('No. Stop.') with steady body; the exit (leave towards people, not paths); no explaining needed - a no requires no essay. Practise until the voice does not shake.

The telling protocol: tell a trusted adult EARLY - parent, teacher, school counsellor - even when afraid, even when the pressurer is known to the family, even when they beg you to keep it. The secret's silence is the pressurer's shield; your voice is your shield.

It is never your fault - said plainly: clothes, walking routes, friendliness - none of it is permission; the adult carrying wrong intentions carries the guilt. Children who tell are protected and praised, not disgraced.

Friends watching over friends: notice the change (withdrawal, gifts appearing, fear of a particular person); walk beside, ask privately, encourage the telling; accompany to the trusted adult if wanted.
Practical safety: walk in company, keep to routes with people, avoid isolated shortcuts at dusk, keep phone access where possible, and keep no secrets that make you afraid.
Home challenge: name your three trusted adults; write your exit-and-tell plan; and if anything unsafe has already touched your life - this week is the week to tell.
activities: Lure-recognition sorting with scenario cards.
Refusal-and-exit role-plays with feedback.
Personal safety plan writing (private).

reallife.situation: An older man begins sending a JHS 2 girl money and messages, asking to meet 'just to talk' where nobody knows them.
reallife.way: Refuse, block, distance - and tell a trusted adult the same week. Gifts with hooks are debts dressed as kindness; the earlier adults know, the faster the pressure dies.

reallife.situation: A boy is pressed by an older 'uncle' for private meetings and told reporting would shame the family.
reallife.way: The shame belongs to the pressurer alone. Tell the trusted adult - the family's protection grows when it knows. Silence is the only thing that ever shamed a victim.

home: Write your exit-and-tell plan and keep it private but ready.
Tell a trusted adult about any pressure that exists now.
Walk in company and keep your routes public where you can.
discussion: Name the four signs of unsafe attention.
Perform the firm-no and exit.
Why is telling early protection and not disgrace?
How do you help a friend under pressure?
resources.assessment: Recognition accuracy. Refusal performance. Plan completeness.
resources.encouragement: Brave, wise and protected - that is what you now are! Your body is yours, your no is complete, and your voice is your fortress. Tell early, stand together, and let no one trade your tomorrow for their appetite. Ayekoo, my guarded champions!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: When You Lose Someone: Living With Grief
resources.why: Almost every class will, sooner or later, lose someone - a grandparent, a parent, a friend - and grief arrives without a syllabus. Students who understand grief's normal shape, and who know how to carry their own and support others, heal sooner and stand by each other properly.
outcomes: Understand that grief brings waves of many feelings - sadness, anger, numbness, guilt - and all are normal.
Express grief healthily: talk, cry, write, remember, pray - and keep eating, sleeping and attending school.
Support a grieving classmate: presence, patience, practical help - and no 'strong up' pressure to perform wellness.
Recognise when grief needs adult help: long silence, talk of self-harm, total withdrawal - and act.
steps: Naming the waves: grief is not one feeling but a sea of them, arriving without order - tears one hour, laughter the next, anger at the world, guilt about words unsaid. The class learns the waves are normal; the sea does not drown those who name it.
The myths corrected: 'big boys do not cry' is a lie that delays healing; 'forget and move on' is not how humans work - we carry the loved one WITH us, not instead of us.
Healthy expression: talk to someone trusted; cry without apology; write letters to the one lost; remember out loud - stories keep the person alive in the family; pray or reflect as your faith guides.

Life continues with love: eating, sleeping, school and play are not betrayals of the dead - they are the vessel that carries the memory forward. The grieving student keeps structure; structure carries the sea.

Supporting a classmate: do not say 'be strong' (they already are); do say 'I am here'; sit near at break; share notes; walk home together; mention the loved one's name - silence pretends the person never lived.
The months talk: grief softens in waves, not on a schedule; anniversaries and photographs strike again - normal; each wave passes sooner.

When to call adults in: if weeks pass with no eating, no sleep, no talk, or any word of self-harm - adults must be told at once; heavy grief sometimes needs professional hands, and seeking them is wisdom.
Home challenge: write (privately) one memory of someone you miss; identify your trusted grief-adult; practise one support act for a grieving classmate this week.
activities: Waves-mapping discussion: naming feelings without shame.
Support-scripts workshop: what to say and do for a grieving friend.
Memory-writing session (private, voluntary sharing).

reallife.situation: A student's father dies; he returns to school numb, is told to 'man up', and stops speaking entirely for weeks.
reallife.way: The class that knows grief does not demand performances. Presence, patience and one honest sentence - 'I am here; we can talk or just sit' - begin the healing that 'man up' delays for years.

reallife.situation: A girl loses her grandmother and carries guilt about the last argument; she stops eating well and hides it.
reallife.way: Guilt is grief in disguise - it needs speaking, not swallowing. A trusted adult helps sort what the waves stir up; eating and school continue, and the sea gradually calms.

home: Write or tell one memory of someone you miss.
Practise one support sentence for a grieving friend.
Tell a trusted adult if grief is stopping your eating, sleep or school.
discussion: Name four feelings grief brings and why all are normal.
What do you say - and not say - to a grieving friend?
Why does structure help the grieving student?
When must adults be called in?
resources.assessment: Waves-mapping participation. Support scripts quality. Memory writing sincerity.
resources.encouragement: Gentle hearts, be comforted! You have learned to carry the heaviest load life assigns - loss - with truth, tears and friends beside you. The waves pass; the love remains. Stand by each other in the sea. Ayekoo, my compassionate ones!
resources.subject: Life Skills

resources.title: Temptation to Cheat: Why Cheating Steals Your Future
resources.why: Around every exam whispers travel: apor, 'expo', copied homework, leaked papers. The cheated mark looks like a rescue - and is actually a theft from your own future: the topic remains unlearned, the next level demands it, and the habit matures into a character. This lesson arms students to refuse and to succeed honestly.
outcomes: Identify the faces of cheating: copying homework, exam apor, ghost-writing, phone malpractice.
Explain the true cost: unlearned topics compound, trust breaks, and consequences follow at school and beyond.
Reject the pressure lines: 'everybody cheats', 'marks matter more', 'the smart ones share answers'.
Choose the honest alternatives: ask, revise, manage time - and accept an honest score as a real starting point.
steps: The faces named: copying a friend's homework; exam leakage ('apor'); whispered answers; phone in the hall; impersonation. Each is cheating - none is 'smartness'.
The compound interest of not learning: today's copied algebra is tomorrow's insoluble equation; BECE copied is SHS survived badly; a certificate without skill is a masked face at every interview.
The consequences plainly: caught cheating in national exams carries real penalties - cancellation, bans, years lost; and even when unseen, the empty head walks with you into every future room.

The pressure lines answered: 'everybody cheats' (everybody's failure is not your plan); 'marks matter more' (marks without learning are a loan shark's receipt); 'help a friend by showing answers' (the cruelest help - it robs the friend of learning).

The honest alternatives, concretely: ask the teacher what to study; use past questions; form the protocol group; manage the fuel; run the exam strategy. Preparation is the real apor - and it cannot be confiscated.
Integrity connection (LS-UP-018): your name in the dark is still your name; the unwatched exam is the real exam.
The comeback reframe: an honest 40 with a comeback plan (LS-UP-014) beats a stolen 80 that collapses at the next level.

Home challenge: write your personal anti-cheating pledge; identify your one weakest exam habit and fix it with the tools taught; report pressures to leak papers - reporting protects the whole class's certificate.
activities: Pressure-line rebuttal drills in pairs.
Consequence mapping: the copied topic traced three years forward.
Honest-preparation plan written and signed.

reallife.situation: A student buys leaked answers, passes BECE, and collapses in SHS where the bought topics resurface as prerequisites.
reallife.way: Apor does not delete the syllabus - it postpones it with interest. The honest struggle now is cheaper than the fake pass forever.

reallife.situation: A pupil copies homework nightly and feels clever until the class test strips the disguise publicly.
reallife.way: Copied homework is borrowed clothes for a naked understanding. Ask, attempt, fail honestly, learn - the honest 40 grows; the disguised 0 stays 0 forever.

home: Sign your anti-cheating plan and display it.
Use the preparation tools on your next test instead of any shortcut.
Report any leakage approaches to a trusted adult promptly.
discussion: Name the four faces of cheating.
Answer the three pressure lines with the taught responses.
Trace a copied topic three years forward - what breaks?
Why is an honest 40 more valuable than a stolen 90?
resources.assessment: Pressure-line responses heard. Plan quality and signature. Discussion contribution.
resources.encouragement: Integrity guarders, hold your line! The honest mark is a true address - it tells you where you really are, and every step from there is really yours. Cheating maps a road to nowhere; honesty maps tomorrow. Walk true. Ayekoo, my trustworthy ones!

resources.title: Anger Management: Cool Heads Win
resources.why: At adolescent intensity, anger arrives with muscle: a word becomes a wound, a shove becomes a case, a rumor becomes a war. The JHS student who can read anger's early signs, cool it fast, and channel it into words and solutions keeps friendships, records and freedom - and leads where others merely burn.
outcomes: Identify personal anger triggers and early body signals.
Apply the cool-down protocol: pause, breathe, move, speak later.
Convert anger into communication: the I-statement and the request.
Repair after an anger explosion: own it, apologise fully, reset the rules.
steps: The anger anatomy: trigger (what lit it) - thoughts (the story we tell) - body (heat, fists, voice) - action (what we do). Control lives between story and action; the earlier you enter, the cheaper the victory.
Personal mapping: each pupil lists private triggers (mockery of family, being accused wrongly, losing unfairly, being touched) and their body signals - the personal alarm system.

The cool-down protocol drilled: 1) PAUSE - one breath before any response. 2) BREATHE - three slow breaths. 3) MOVE - create distance. 4) SPEAK LATER - the words can wait; the regret cannot be unsaid.
The I-statement practised: 'I felt humiliated when you said that in front of the class. I ask you not to do it again.' - anger converted into a message that can actually change things.
The escalation ladder named and refused: silence-to-violence paths (stare, shove, blow) all begin with steps that can be stopped at step one; the cool head exits the ladder early.
Repair after eruption: the four-part apology (LS-UP-019's formula), the wound tended, the boundary agreed; a repaired friendship with new rules outlasts the war.
Channels for the fire: sport, writing, talking to a trusted adult, faith practice - anger is energy; energy needs a chosen direction.
Home challenge: map your triggers; run the protocol in real life once this week; perform one repair if needed; report privately Friday.
activities: Trigger-mapping personal worksheets.
Protocol drill against staged provocations.
I-statement conversions from raw anger sentences.

reallife.situation: A classmate mocks a boy's mother; he shoves, a fight follows, and both stand before disciplinary punishment - the original insult now forgotten.
reallife.way: Pause at step one: breath, distance, then the I-statement or the teacher. The shove converts him from insulted to punished - the cool head keeps both dignity and record.

reallife.situation: A girl erupts at home over a rumour, breaks a cup, and carries a week's silence with her mother.
reallife.way: The protocol works at home too: pause, breathe, then the honest sentence. The cup can be replaced; the repair must be made with the four parts and a changed tone.

home: Map your personal triggers and body signals.
Apply the cool-down protocol once in real life this week.
Make one repair with the four-part apology if needed.
discussion: Explain the trigger-body-story-action chain.
Perform the I-statement conversion.
Why does exiting early win?
How is an anger explosion repaired?
resources.assessment: Mapping completeness. Drill performance. Repair reports (private).
resources.encouragement: Cool heads, strong hands - that is the champion's combination! You now hold the protocol that turns wildfire into working steam. Map your triggers, pause at the alarm, speak your case. The one who rules his own anger rules the room. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Good Friends vs Bad Company: The Company Test
resources.why: In JHS, company begins to decide outcomes: the group you keep writes your habits, your talk, your risks - and your results. Building on LS-UP-018, this lesson sharpens the company test for adolescents, where the stakes (alcohol, betting, advances, exam malpractice) are far higher.
outcomes: Apply the company test to current friendships: where does this company carry me?
Recognise adolescent-grade red flags: pressure to bet, drink, abscond, cheat, or hide from parents.
Exit bad company firmly and politely - and survive the loneliness phase.
Build a deliberate inner circle that matches your destination.
steps: The adolescent stakes named: at this level, bad company is not just noise - it carries fees (betting losses, police cases, pregnancy scares, exam bans). The company question is now a destiny question.

The company test taught and applied privately to each pupil's five closest companions: 1) After being with them, are my marks, manners and peace up or down? 2) What do we talk about most - plans or play? 3) Do they cheer my discipline or mock it? 4) Where do they want to carry me - name the place.

The red flags rolled out: 'just try it once'; 'hide this from your mother'; 'you are too serious - relax'; pressure that multiplies when refused; friends who appear only when money or mischief appears.
The exit protocol drilled: reduce the time, refuse the invitations plainly, never mock them (respect preserves peace), and let repetition do the quiet work. No war needed - a consistent no is louder.

The loneliness season addressed honestly: leaving a gang feels like a fast for a few weeks - plan the replacements (study group, sports, youth fellowship, library); the emptiness is temporary, the direction is permanent.
The inner circle design: choose 3-5 by destination - people whose plans you would be proud to inherit; write the qualities; begin investing in those friendships deliberately.
The return question: some old company may reform - keep the door open for the changed, with the rules agreed; wisdom keeps the bridge and holds the boundary.
Home challenge: run the test on your five privately; choose your circle; perform one polite refusal this week and report privately.
activities: Company test personal audit (private, no names shared).
Red-flag scenario sorting for adolescents.
Inner-circle design workshop with destination matching.

reallife.situation: A boy's closest group begins with betting talk, graduates to alcohol at weekend joints, and mocks every study plan.
reallife.way: The circle is the current - swim against it weekly or be carried. Name it, reduce it, replace it; the destination you wrote deserves a crew rowing the same way.

reallife.situation: A girl's 'bestie' pressures her to lie to her mother about whereabouts and mocks her refusal.
reallife.way: A friend who requires your mother's deception has already priced your trust. Exit politely, replace deliberately, and let the loneliness season pass - it always does.

home: Audit five close companions privately with the company test.
Invest in one building friendship this week.
Perform one polite, firm refusal and log it.
discussion: Run the four company-test questions aloud.
Name three adolescent-grade red flags.
How does one survive the loneliness season?
How is an inner circle designed?
resources.assessment: Audit honesty. Scenario analysis quality. Refusal performance.
resources.encouragement: Circle builders, choose like generals! Company is destiny's draft - pick those who march to your drumbeat or march alone awhile until they appear. Your JHS 3 self will thank the circle you choose today. Ayekoo, my deliberate ones!

resources.title: Saying No Without Losing Friends
resources.why: Most adolescent trouble begins as a yes said to keep a friend. Saying no without war - and without losing the friendship that deserves to survive - is a learnable art of tone, timing and truth. The pupil who masters it keeps both the friend and the future.
outcomes: Distinguish refusals that preserve friendship from refusals that start wars.
Use the structured refusal: value, no, alternative, and - if pressed - the firm close.
Manage the mockery phase: calm repetition, humour where fitting, exit when needed.
Recognise when 'losing the friend' is actually losing the trap.
steps: The anatomy of a good no: 1) THE VALUE - 'I am not into that' or 'I have my BECE plan'. 2) THE NO - plain, without a essay of excuses (excuses invite counter-offers). 3) THE ALTERNATIVE - 'let us go and play football instead'. 4) THE CLOSE - if pressed: same no, calmer voice, standing still.

Tone and body: the no said while smiling and joking half-heartedly invites a second offer; the no said with steady eyes and a settled body ends negotiations. Practice on both until the difference is felt.

The mockery phase prepared for: 'you are scared', 'chop small, nobody will know' - the responses: repeat the no without new reasons; light deflection ('my mother's eyes are CCTV'); walk if it persists. Repetition is the refusal's backbone.
The friendship arithmetic: a friend who accepts your no is a keeper; a friend who ends the friendship over one no was already pricing your freedom cheaply - the loss is a release, not a tragedy.

Soft nos in daily life: refusing to copy homework ('let me teach you instead'), refusing to cover for lateness, refusing to mock a classmate - the same structure, gentler tone; most friendships survive a respectful no with an alternative offered.
When the no must be final: persistent pressure on drink, drugs, advances or crime is not friendship - it is recruitment. Name it, refuse it, and walk with your dignity intact.
The ally approach: pair up before the party - two nos are harder to crack than one; agree signals with a like-minded friend in advance.
Home challenge: use the structured refusal in real life twice this week (once soft, once firm); report privately how it went.
activities: Refusal-building workshop: value, no, alternative, close.
Tone-and-body rehearsal: the joking no versus the settled no.
Mockery-phase drill with repetition practice.

reallife.situation: Friends press a girl to skip prep and join a night stroll 'just this once'.
reallife.way: The value, the plain no, the alternative ('prep now, walk on Saturday'), and the calm repetition. The friendship that respects her prep was real; the one that dies over prep was a queue.

reallife.situation: A boy is mocked daily for refusing betting: 'fear catch you?'
reallife.way: Repeat the no, keep the tone level, and let time testify - the mockers' pockets will do the final lecturing. Peace kept, pocket kept, dignity kept.

home: Practise the four-part refusal aloud until fluent.
Agree an ally signal with one like-minded friend.
Perform two real refusals this week and report privately.
discussion: Recite the four-part refusal.
Demonstrate the settled-no body language.
Why is repetition stronger than new excuses?
When is 'losing a friend' actually a release?
resources.assessment: Refusal structure performance. Mockery-phase drill. Ally agreement quality.
resources.encouragement: No-sayers with warm hearts, well done! You have learned to guard your future without burning your friendships - the rarest social art. Repeat the no until it is music, hold your allies close, and lose only the traps. Ayekoo, my graceful refusers!

resources.title: Teamwork That Wins: Group Work and Leadership
resources.why: From group assignments to BECE projects, from sports teams to future workplaces, results come through others. Students who can divide work fairly, keep people moving, and disagree without war become the captains every team seeks - a skill with rules, practiseable today.
outcomes: Organise group work: clear goal, divided tasks with names, agreed deadline, check-in points.
Contribute dependably: do your part to standard, communicate delays early.
Disagree with respect: attack the idea, not the person; seek the merged solution.
Lead without bossing: model the standard, assign by strength, carry the quiet members.
steps: The anatomy of a working group taught: one GOAL written down; tasks divided BY NAME with deadlines; a check-in point agreed; a finisher who assembles the parts.

The division protocol: list the tasks, match tasks to strengths where possible (the artist draws, the talker presents, the careful one writes), set realistic deadlines, write it all where all can see.
The dependable contributor's code: do your part early, not the night before assembly; flag delays at once ('I cannot finish my part - can we adjust?'); never let silence sink the group.

Disagreement protocol: the idea may be attacked; the person may not. Phrases taught: 'I see it differently - what if we...?', 'Can we test both ideas?', 'Let us merge both.' Personal war dissolved by merged solutions.

Leadership practised, not lectured: the good leader works hardest, assigns fairly, listens to the quiet member (who often holds the best idea), and says thank you publicly. Bossing by shouting produces silence and sabotage; leading by example produces volunteers.

Handling the free rider: private friendly reminder first ('we need your part by Friday - can you manage?'), then the team adjusts visibly and informs the teacher early - never ambush the free-rider in public; give accountability a face-saving door.
The presentation prep: one voice or shared voices with one message; rehearse once fully timed; a group that practises once presents with peace.
Home challenge: run one real group task this week with the full protocol - goal, names, deadline, check-in, assembly; assess honestly and report.
activities: Group-formation exercise with the division protocol on a real task.
Disagreement-to-merge role-plays.
Assembly rehearsal with timed presentation.

reallife.situation: A five-member assignment: two work, two hide, one dominates; the grade collapses and friendships bruise.
reallife.way: The division protocol prevents all three failures: tasks by name, deadlines visible, delays announced early, the dominator reminded gently, the teacher informed early when needed.

reallife.situation: Two group members quarrel over whose idea stands and the work freezes for a week.
reallife.way: Attack the idea, not the person; then merge - the merged idea is usually stronger than either original. The freeze ends when the goal is re-read aloud together.

home: Organise one real group task with the full protocol this week.
Practise one respectful disagreement in the group.
Report the process and result honestly Friday.
discussion: Recite the group-work anatomy.
Demonstrate respectful disagreement with a phrase.
How is a free rider handled with dignity?
What makes a leader worth following?
resources.assessment: Task organisation quality. Disagreement handling observed. Assembly and presentation standard.
resources.encouragement: Team builders and leaders, well done! You now know the secret of all great works: fair division, early words, respect in disagreement, and leadership that carries the quiet ones. Practise it here, and every future team will be glad you came. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Online Scams: Beyond the Basics
resources.why: Building on MoMo safety (LS-FIN-004), today's scammers run a wider industry: fake promotions, 'instant job' offers, romance hooks, cloned VIP links. The JHS student is a prime target - new to money, hungry for opportunity. One trained reflex - verify before you trust - repels most of the industry.
outcomes: Recognise the major scam families: fake promotions, MoMo fraud, job and scholarship scams, romance hooks, phishing links.
Apply the verification reflex: slow down, verify independently, never share codes or PINs.
Protect accounts: strong passwords, two-step where possible, no codes shared - ever.
Know the reporting path: platform, adult, and police (CID/eyewitness reports) when money is involved.
steps: The scam families toured with real-style examples: 'You have won a promo - pay activation fee'; 'Your MoMo will expire - send to this number'; job/scholarship forms collecting fees and ID photos; 'I love you, help me with an emergency' from a stranger online; links that mimic bank or network sites.

The universal tells: urgency ('now or never'); secrecy ('do not tell your parents'); pay-first-then-receive; codes and PINs requested; too-good offers (a phone for 50 cedis). Speed, silence and payment are the three red flags in almost every scam.

The verification reflex drilled: 1) PAUSE - no decision in excitement or fear. 2) VERIFY - call the official line yourself (find it, do not use the number in the message); ask a parent or teacher. 3) PROTECT - codes, PINs, IDs and passwords are never shared, even with friends.
Link hygiene: hover/long-press to preview; check the real address; never sign in from a link that arrived by message; type the official site yourself.
The 'too good' law: free money, doubling money, easy jobs for students - the internet's too-good offers arehooks; real opportunities charge no fees to strangers and verify you, not your purse.
What if you already sent money? Tell an adult immediately - speed matters for telecom/blocking interventions; report to police for record; the shame of reporting is lighter than the loss of silence.
Account armour: unique passwords (not birthdays), two-step verification where offered, logout on shared devices, and never saving PINs in notes.
Home challenge: audit one recent message that smelled off and trace its tricks; rehearse the three-step reflex; secure one account tonight.
activities: Scam autopsy workshop: dissect five sample messages and name the tricks.
Verification reflex drill against staged offers.
Account-armour practical: password and two-step setup.

reallife.situation: A student receives 'Your MoMo account will be blocked in 2 hours - send your PIN to reactivate' and loses a term's savings in minutes.
reallife.way: The countdown is the weapon - urgency is the pickpocket's clock. Pause, verify through an official channel you found yourself, and never surrender a PIN to any message, ever.

reallife.situation: A boy pays a 'registration fee' for an online scholarship and the collector vanishes after his ID photos arrive.
reallife.way: Real scholarships collect documents, not fees, and verify through official sites. Where fees precede promises, pause - and let a teacher's eyes read the offer before any money moves.

home: Dissect one suspicious message this week and name its tricks.
Rehearse pause - verify - protect until automatic.
Secure one account with a strong password and two-step if available.
discussion: List the universal scam signals.
Perform the three-step reflex aloud.
Why never sign in from a message link?
What is the first move after money is already sent?
resources.assessment: Scam autopsy quality. Reflex rehearsal. Account security completed.
resources.encouragement: Scam-proof and sharp - that is you now! The fraud industry spends its genius on the hasty; your pause makes their tricks homeless. Verify before you trust, protect your codes, and let the scammers starve. Ayekoo, my alert ones!

resources.title: Your Digital Footprint and Your Future
resources.why: Everything posted online is a permanent exhibit: screenshots outlive deletions, and admissions officers, employers and partners eventually meet your history. The JHS student who posts wisely today protects scholarships, jobs and reputation years before they are needed.
outcomes: Understand the permanence rule: the internet forgets nothing - deletion removes your copy, not the copies.
Audit your own digital footprint honestly and privately.
Apply the future-filter before posting: would this survive my grandparents', a headmaster's and an employer's eyes?
Practise the repair protocol: delete, correct, apologise, and let good conduct rebuild.
steps: The permanence truth: delete removes your view; screenshots and archives keep theirs. Posts travel - the private joke forwarded becomes the public exhibit; the angry rant screenshotted follows its author into interviews.
The footprint tour: what the internet already holds of a typical student - photos, comments, tags by friends, group chats exported. Discussion: which exhibits would you frame, which would you burn?

The future-filter taught: before posting ask three questions - 1) Would I show this to my headmaster or grandmother? 2) Would a scholarship panel respect it? 3) Does it hurt anyone? If any answer wavers, do not post.

Naked-trust dangers said plainly: intimate images sent 'privately' become weapons in every falling-out; the sender never controls the receiver's hands. Never create what you could not survive owning publicly.

Repair protocol drilled: 1) DELETE - remove what you control. 2) ASK - request friends remove or correct posts about you. 3) OWN - if it leaked, tell the trusted adult first, before the internet completes its arithmetic. 4) REBUILD - a year of good posts buries a bad week; the feed is a garden, tend it.
Privacy settings as routine: who sees what, checked termly; location sharing off; group chats audited for what is said 'in confidence'.
Friend-tagging discipline: your tag is your signature - do not appear in what you would not post; ask friends to remove exhibits of you you regret.
Home challenge: complete a private footprint audit tonight; perform one repair (delete, ask, correct); set one privacy upgrade; report only what you choose.
activities: Private footprint audit with a personal checklist.
Post-or-never decision drills on grey-area posts.
Repair protocol rehearsal in three scenarios.

reallife.situation: A boy's year-old insulting post surfaces when he is shortlisted for a scholarship; the panel asks about character.
reallife.way: The internet keeps receipts; audit yours before others audit them for you. Delete, explain honestly, and let a year of good exhibits rewrite the summary.

reallife.situation: An intimate image shared 'in trust' spreads through three schools in a week.
reallife.way: Never create what you cannot own - the receiver's hands are not yours to command. If it happens, tell the trusted adult immediately: adults can act; silence only feeds the fire.

home: Run a private footprint audit with the checklist.
Perform one repair: delete, request a correction, or adjust privacy.
Write your three-question future-filter and keep it visible.
discussion: Explain the permanence rule with the screenshot example.
State the three future-filter questions.
Why are 'private' intimate images never safe?
What are the four steps of the repair protocol?
resources.assessment: Audit completion (private). Decision-drill accuracy. Repair executed.
resources.encouragement: Gardeners of your online name, tend well! Every post is a seed - plant what your future self will harvest with pride. Screenshots outlive moods; let your feed speak well of you in rooms you have not entered yet. Ayekoo, my wise planters!

resources.title: Travel Smart: Trotro, Roads and Night Movement
resources.why: JHS students now move alone more than ever: trotro to school, roads to town, occasional night movement for church or family events. Alert habits - where you sit, what you announce, when you move - separate the student who arrives from the one who becomes a story.
outcomes: Practise road-crossing and walking discipline as an adolescent (phones away, eyes up, bridges where they exist).
Use trotro wisely: know your stop, keep valuables low-key, mind belongings, refuse overloading shortcuts.
Announce movements: parents always know where and with whom; late movements need prior permission.
Handle night movement with extra rules: company, light, known routes, no shortcuts.
steps: The walking protocol: face traffic where roads allow; phones in the pocket, not the palm (heads-up walkers miss danger); cross at designated points; assume drivers cannot see you - make yourself visible and predictable.

Trotro wisdom: know your stop before boarding; sit where exits are visible; keep your bag on your lap, phone out of sight; if the mate shouts 'we are full, jump in', the overloaded vehicle is not your vehicle.

The movement announcement: parents or guardians always know where you are going, with whom, and when you should return; plans change - a message updates them. The student whose family never has to search is the student who announces.
Night movement rules: avoid it where possible; where unavoidable - company, main roads, lit paths, no shortcuts through bushes or uncompleted buildings; a call home on arrival.
The lift question: never enter private vehicles offering rides; where a lift is truly arranged, it is arranged by parents - not by charm at the roadside.
Strangers and stories: the traveller's kindness tests - helping is fine in public places among people; private directions into quiet corners are refused without apology.
Money and valuables low-key: phones pocketed at stops, earrings turned in crowds, counting money in the open road is an advertisement - count in safety.
Home challenge: agree your route and rules with parents this week; practise the announcement habit; walk one route consciously applying the protocol.
activities: Route-audit exercise: map your regular routes and mark risk points.
Trotro role-play: boarding, stop awareness, low-key valuables.
Night-movement protocol checklist design.

reallife.situation: A student crosses while typing a message and a bike she never saw clips her bag.
reallife.way: Eyes up, phone pocketed, cross at the points designed for it. The message can wait; the leg may not.

reallife.situation: Two students accept a 'shortcut lift' from a friendly driver at dusk and arrive somewhere entirely different.
reallife.way: Lifts are arranged by parents or not taken at all; shortcuts through silence are how stories go wrong. Known routes, company, and announced movements are the traveller's armour.

home: Agree your routes and movement rules with your parents this week.
Practise the announcement habit for every movement.
Apply the night rules on your next unavoidable night movement.
discussion: Recite the walking protocol.
Demonstrate low-key trotro behaviour.
Why is the announcement habit protection?
What are the night-movement rules?
resources.assessment: Route audit quality. Role-play performance. Checklist completion.
resources.encouragement: Travellers, move wisely! Alert eyes, announced plans and steady routes carry you home every time. The road respects the careful student - be that one. Ayekoo, my travelling champions!

resources.title: Growing Up: Body Changes and Cleanliness for Boys and Girls
resources.why: JHS bodies are changing fast - voice, hair, sweat, periods, new feelings - and the yard fills with half-truths where the classroom should speak plainly. Students who understand their changing bodies, keep the upgraded hygiene, and respect everyone else's changes, walk through adolescence with dignity.
outcomes: Describe the normal changes of puberty for boys and girls without embarrassment or myth.
Maintain the adolescent hygiene routine: daily bathing with soap on all zones, fresh underwear daily, footwear care, breath care.
Manage menstruation knowledgeably and respectfully (for all students, not only girls).
Ask private questions of trusted adults and refuse the yard's mythology.
steps: Puberty named calmly: it is the body's planned construction, not a sickness or a secret - voice changes, hair growth, sweat increase, periods, new feelings. Everyone's timetable differs; all are normal.
The myth sweep: the yard's claims examined and corrected with facts; the rule agreed - questions go to trusted adults (parents, school nurse, teachers), never to rumour.

Menstruation for everyone: what it is, why it is normal and healthy, how girls manage it practically (pads, washing, disposal in the proper way, school support where needed) - and why boys' role is respect: no jokes, no teasing, practical help where needed (carrying, escorting, calling the nurse).

Hygiene upgraded for adolescents: soap on underarms, feet and private areas daily; underwear daily; uniforms washed regularly; socks and footwear dried; water intake; clean towels and combs never shared.
Wet dreams, discharge and other normal events discussed factually - clean, dry, unhurried; nothing to fear, much to ask; the body's plumbing deserves calm information, not panic.
Respect charter: body changes are never mocked; growing early or late is nobody's fault or comedy; the class agrees and signs.
Feelings and confusions get a route too: trusted adults answer what the yard cannot; asking is courage, not weakness.
Home challenge: run the adolescent routine seven days; bring one written private question (anonymous box accepted); sign the charter.
activities: Question-box session: written questions answered honestly and respectfully.
Puberty-fact matching for boys and girls.
Respect charter drafting and signing.

reallife.situation: A girl's first period arrives at school unannounced; the class that was taught responds with help, not laughter.
reallife.way: The taught class carries pads, calls the nurse quietly, and stands guard over her dignity. Knowledge in every student - boys included - is what turns panic into a managed moment.

reallife.situation: A boy's voice cracks in an exam and the hall giggles; he shrinks for weeks.
reallife.way: The charter class knows the timetable: everyone's body builds at its own hour. No jokes, no nicknames - and the boy learns his body is on schedule, not on trial.

home: Run the full adolescent hygiene routine for seven days.
Submit one private question this week (anonymous box available).
Uphold the respect charter daily.
discussion: Describe puberty as construction, not sickness.
Explain menstruation factually - and the boys' duty of respect.
Which hygiene zones need daily soap and why dry well?
Where do private questions go, and why not the yard?
resources.assessment: Question quality (anonymous accepted). Charter signing. Routine checklists.
resources.encouragement: Growing men and women of dignity, well done! You have learned the truth about your own construction - and the respect that makes everyone's journey safe. Ask your questions bravely, keep your cleanliness high, and honour every classmate's timetable. Ayekoo!

resources.title: Volunteerism: The Ghanaian Spirit of Helping Free
resources.why: Long before salaries, Ghanaian communities were carried by free hands: the communal labour, the funeral kitchen, the flood rescue. Students who volunteer learn skills, build names, and join a tradition that opens doors - helping freely is how value is proven before it is paid.
outcomes: Explain volunteerism as a Ghanaian tradition and its place in community life.
Plan and execute one real volunteer act: in school, church/mosque, or community.
Record and reflect on what volunteering taught - skills, contacts, reputation.
Balance service with schoolwork and healthy motives (service, not showmanship).
steps: The tradition opened: communal labour swept compounds and built schools long before contracts existed; the family that fed funeral guests free; the boys who cleared the flooded gutter. Free hands built the trust that paid hands later inherited.

What volunteering builds in YOU: skills (organising, cooking for crowds, speaking), visibility (elders remember the boy who carried water at dawn), networks (the church elder who later signs your form), and character tested where nobody pays.
The opportunity map built with the class: school events, clean-up campaigns, funeral and wedding support (with family), church/mosque programmes, community health walks, helping the aged neighbour.
The service standard: work given as if paid - punctual, complete, cheerful; the free job done poorly advertises the wrong name.
Motives audited: service seeks no cameras; the helper who posts everything is serving the post. Serve where the need is, not where the audience is.
The schoolwork guard: volunteering fills free hours, never study hours; a boy whose service starves his marks has confused his ladder.
The record habit: keep a service diary - what, when, skills gained, people met. Future applications, references and even scholarships ask exactly these questions.
Home challenge: complete one real volunteer act this week (chosen from the map), record it with a reflection, and report Friday.
activities: Opportunity-mapping workshop for your own community.
Service diary setup with reflection format.
One executed volunteer act with a written reflection.

reallife.situation: Two students need a recommendation: one has a service diary - swept the clinic compound monthly, helped at immunisation days; the other has none.
reallife.way: Free hands had already written the letter before anyone asked. Volunteering is CV construction disguised as kindness - and the disguise is sincere.

reallife.situation: A student volunteers only when visitors or cameras appear, and vanishes when it is merely work.
reallife.way: Service performed for the stage is theatre; the community measures the unwatched hours. Serve where nobody claps - that is where the real name is minted.

home: Complete one real volunteer act this week.
Record it in the service diary with a reflection.
Plan your next month's service opportunity.
discussion: What does volunteering build in the volunteer?
Why is the unwatched act the valuable one?
Map three service opportunities near you.
How does service balance with schoolwork?
resources.assessment: Volunteer act completed and documented. Reflection sincerity. Planning quality.
resources.encouragement: Servers of the community, well done! The free hand you lend today is the signature tomorrow's opportunities will search for. Serve sincerely, record honestly, and let your name travel ahead of you. Ayekoo, my generous ones!

resources.title: Plastics in Our Drains: Community Action
resources.why: Every rainy season, Ghana's cities drown in water that has nowhere to go - blocked by sachets and bottles thrown carelessly for months. The JHS student who understands the chain - litter, drain, flood, cholera - and acts locally turns from bystander to builder.
outcomes: Trace the litter-to-flood chain: dropped sachet, blocked gutter, flooded street, sick community.
Practise the reduce-reuse-recycle hierarchy at home and school level.
Plan and run one community or school anti-plastic action.
Influence others: family, friends, market practices - one trained student is a campaign.
steps: The chain traced slowly: one sachet dropped in a gutter joins thousands; the drain narrows; the first heavy rain climbs the banks; shops flood, gutters breed mosquitoes, cholera follows. One drop of litter, one street of consequences.

The waste hierarchy taught: REFUSE first (do you need another bag?), REDUCE (refill bottles, carry bags), REUSE (sachets and bottles become planters, scoops, art), RECYCLE (where collection exists) - and disposal only as the last resort, done properly.
The local audit: pupils map their own streets - where litter gathers, which drains choke first, who disposes properly and who does not.

The action plan built: one school or community target (a drain, a market path, a school compound), the team, the tools, the timeline, the safety rules (no touching sharps barehanded, gloves where possible, wash up after).
The influence skills: how to speak to a family member about their plastic habit without quarrels - the example first, the word second, the invitation third ('join me this Saturday').
The alternatives practised: cloth bags for market, refillable bottles where water is safe, saying no to double-bagging - refusal is the cheapest recycling.
Community voices: invited speaker or elder discusses how the community handled floods before plastics, and what changed - history as evidence.
Home challenge: run one anti-plastic action this week (a clean-up, a home audit, a persuasion campaign) and document before-and-after.
activities: Litter-trace walk around the school: map where the chain begins.
Reuse workshop: bottles and sachets turned into planters and scoops.
One executed community action with documentation.

reallife.situation: A rainy season floods the market street; traders lose goods; the children wade to school - all traced to a season of dropped sachets.
reallife.way: The flood began in careless hands months earlier. The street that bins its plastics keeps its market dry - and the trained child is the street's first teacher.

reallife.situation: A student mocks clean-up days as 'small' and drops a sachet while walking - which a classmate quietly picks up.
reallife.way: No act of litter is small; no refusal is small either. The compound's character is the sum of ten thousand private decisions - make yours count where nobody watches.

home: Audit your home's plastic use for one week and change three habits.
Join or run one community anti-plastic action.
Persuade one family member - record how it went.
discussion: Trace the sachet's journey from your hand to the flood.
Recite the waste hierarchy with examples.
How do you persuade without quarrels?
What action will you run this week?
resources.assessment: Audit quality. Workshop participation. Action documentation.
resources.encouragement: Drain defenders and street teachers, well done! The flood that never comes is the reward of a thousand small refusals - and you have joined the ranks of those who refuse. Lead your homes, teach your streets. Ayekoo, my community champions!

resources.title: Cyberbullying: Block, Record, Report
resources.why: The bullying that used to end at the school gate now follows children home through phones: groupchat humiliation, fake accounts, circulated shaming. Students who know the three-move defence - block, record, report - survive it with dignity, and schools that train it end its culture.
outcomes: Recognise cyberbullying in its forms: mockery posts, fake accounts, exclusion, circulation of private material, threats.
Apply the three-move protocol: block the bully, record the evidence, report to adults and platforms.
Refuse the bystander roles: never forward, never like, never laugh - the audience is the bully's fuel.
Care for the targeted friend: private support, evidence help, adult accompaniment.
steps: The forms named with examples: the mock post about a classmate; the fake account in a pupil's name; the screenshot circulated from a private chat; the 'roast' that only one child endures; threats and impersonations.
Why online bullying bites harder: no closing bell - it follows home; the audience is silent-invisible so courage drains; deletions leave screenshots; one post can recruit thousands of eyes overnight.

The three moves drilled: 1) BLOCK - cut the channel; do not negotiate with poison. 2) RECORD - screenshot before blocking (evidence beats memory; delete nothing of your own evidence). 3) REPORT - to a trusted adult the same day, and to the platform's report tools; serious cases (threats, circulated private images) go to adults who involve DOVVSU/police where needed.
The retaliation trap exposed: answering with insults converts the victim into a second bully - the record then shows two fighters; the disciplined victim keeps the clean record and the moral ground.

The bystander's oath: forwarding is participating; laughing is auditioning to be next. The trained student: does not share, sends support privately, helps preserve evidence, and walks the friend to the trusted adult.
The victim's dignity preserved: being targeted is not disgrace - the disgrace belongs to the poster; the victim who tells early is protected, not pitied.
Platform literacy: how reporting works on common platforms; privacy tightening after an attack; when to simply leave a poisoned group entirely.
Home challenge: rehearse the three moves until they are reflexes; audit your group memberships; support one rule on your class groups - no mockery content.
activities: Protocol drill: staged cyberbullying scenarios resolved with block - record - report.
Bystander-audit: pupils identify their own forwarding habits and pledge.
Platform-report walkthrough where devices allow.

reallife.situation: A girl's embarrassing photo circulates in a school group with mocking captions; she stops attending.
reallife.way: She must not fight the crowd with crowd-weapons: block, screenshot everything with names visible, and report to the teacher the same day. The class that was taught this protocol ends the circulation by refusing to forward - and the shame lands where it belongs, on the poster.

reallife.situation: A boy discovers a fake account in his name posting insults; panic tempts him to fight the account with insults of his own.
reallife.way: Record first (screenshots with dates), report to the platform for impersonation, and let adults confront the source. Two insulters cannot be told apart; one record and one calm report can.

home: Rehearse the three moves until they are reflexes.
Audit one group you belong to; leave or clean where needed.
Support one targeted friend with the full protocol if it arises - or report what you have seen already.
discussion: Name the forms of cyberbullying you have actually seen.
Perform the three moves in order and explain each.
Why does answering insults keep the war alive?
What makes a bystander's forward button dangerous?
resources.assessment: Protocol drills performed. Bystander analysis quality. Audit completed.
resources.encouragement: Peacekeepers of the feeds, stand ready! The three moves - block, record, report - turn the online jungle into a policed street. Never feed the poison with your own venom; keep the record clean and the adults informed. Ayekoo, my digital defenders!
